OpenProblemBench reports judge-assessed model progress on 82 unresolved mathematics and physics problems Desk: evaluation_science Evidence: A · credible_unconfirmed · active · importance 6/10 (Major) Importance rationale: If the benchmark and judgments are valid, it offers a structured way to compare AI systems on unresolved theoretical research questions, including assessed partial progress rather than answer-key accuracy alone. This could change evaluation priorities for research agents. The reported solve rates are evaluator judgments on one run per model/problem, not expert-validated discoveries or evidence of general autonomous research capability. What changed: OpenProblemBench tests seven model-execution configurations on 82 literature-grounded unresolved questions in mathematics and theoretical physics. Four evaluator models review each frozen solution against explicit proof or computational obligations and score solved, partial or unsolved progress. The paper reports a 14.02% evaluator-averaged solve rate for GPT-6-Astra and 2.44–7.01% for the other configurations; substantive partial progress is also counted. These are author-reported evaluator judgments, not domain-expert validation of discoveries. The authors identify evaluator error correlation, uneven problem coverage, single runs per condition and varying execution resources as limitations. Why it matters: Most AI reasoning benchmarks have known answers, while research often concerns questions without a reference solution. A benchmark that supplies literature context and evaluates proof obligations, computational checks and partial progress could improve how research-agent capability is measured. Here the headline solve rates come from model judges, and the paper itself calls for blinded expert validation; they do not establish that the models made verified scientific discoveries. Demonstrated: The preprint describes the benchmark composition, evaluation protocol, solver configurations and reported review counts/results. The reported correctness and novelty judgments have not been independently established in this review. Claimed: The authors report a 14.02% mean judged solve rate and 84.45% solved-or-substantive-partial share for GPT-6-Astra, with lower judged solve rates for other configurations. These are model-evaluator outcomes, not expert-confirmed solution rates. Mechanism: The benchmark supplies each solver a literature-grounded open problem, assumptions, prior progress and resolution obligations. Four model evaluators separately inspect each frozen submission, check its decisive proof or computation and label solved, partial or unsolved progress; they also flag overclaims. Strongest baseline: The strongest comparison is the same 82 problem statements evaluated across seven solver-execution configurations using the same four evaluator models and shared outcome definitions. A paired Qwen3.8-Max comparison varies harness and web access; the design does not isolate model weights from every execution-system difference. Regime: 82 items: 46 mathematics and 36 theoretical physics. Seven solver-execution configurations produce 574 submissions and 2,296 primary evaluator reviews. Primary solver access disables web retrieval; a paired Qwen3.8-Max harness/web comparison covers the same items. Each condition uses one final run, with up to 12 hours allowed but realized resources varying. Limitations: All solve and partial-progress rates are judgments by four models; independent domain-expert review is needed to establish correctness and novelty, and evaluator agreement does not estimate shared false-positive or false-negative rates.; The benchmark contains 82 selected mathematics and theoretical-physics questions, with uneven subfield composition and comparatively checkable resolution criteria; it does not represent all sciences or all research work.; There is one final run per model/problem condition. Execution harnesses, resource use and historical run conditions vary, so fine performance differences and run-to-run reliability are not established.; Literature review can miss later solutions, and a problem statement or relevant result may occur in model training data. The paper does not establish generalization to new problems or deployed research programs. Contrary evidence: The paper reports that evaluator judgments vary and that rankings below the top configuration are less stable. It explicitly says evaluator agreement alone cannot estimate error rates and calls for blinded expert review.; The benchmark itself shows execution-context sensitivity: a paired harness change altered Qwen3.8-Max outcomes, and web access changed partial-progress judgments without changing the judged solve count in the reported comparison.; The 82 questions are selected for comparatively clear checking and are uneven across fields; success rates cannot be generalized to broad scientific discovery. Open evidence gaps: No blinded expert audit of judged-solved submissions, correctness, novelty or evaluator false-positive rates was available in this review.; One final run per configuration and varying harness/resource conditions leave run-to-run variance and model-versus-execution effects unresolved. Sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.11118v1 3. DFlash reports parallel diffusion drafting for multi-fold speculative decoding speedups Desk: inference_systems Evidence: A · credible_unconfirmed · active · importance 6/10 (Major) Importance rationale: If the reported results reproduce, conditioning a parallel block-diffusion drafter on target-model features could materially reduce decode latency while preserving target outputs across several model/task regimes. This is major inference-engineering evidence, but results are author-run on selected workloads and H200 hardware; deployed throughput, broad hardware transfer and independent reproduction remain open. What changed: DFlash uses a small block-diffusion model to draft multiple tokens in parallel, conditioned on hidden features extracted from a frozen autoregressive target model and injected into the drafter's key/value cache. The ICML 2026 paper reports lossless speculative decoding speedups on selected Qwen3 and Llama models and math, coding and chat workloads; on Qwen3 4B/8B it reports 4.91×/4.86× average speedup at temperature 0 and 4.24×/4.03× at temperature 1 on H200 GPUs. These are author-reported measurements, not an independent reproduction or fleet-throughput result. The paper provides code and checkpoint links, and a public repository describes further serving integrations that were not tested here. Why it matters: Decode latency limits the cost and throughput of reasoning and interactive generation. If target-conditioned diffusion drafting preserves exact target outputs while reducing end-to-end latency in real serving workloads, it could materially improve inference capacity without changing the served model's output distribution. The paper reports promising selected benchmarks, while production concurrency, hardware transfer, full resource costs and independent reproduction remain open. Demonstrated: The paper and public repository disclose the architecture, experimental setup, reported speed measurements, source code link and checkpoint link. This review did not execute code or demonstrate measured speedups independently. Claimed: The authors report lossless decoding acceleration exceeding 6× in selected cases and average Qwen3 4B/8B speedups of 4.91×/4.86× at temperature 0 and 4.24×/4.03× at temperature 1 across the listed task suite. Results vary by task and setting and were not independently reproduced. Mechanism: A lightweight block-diffusion drafter predicts a token block in parallel. Hidden representations sampled from the frozen target model are fused and injected into each draft layer's key/value cache, supplying persistent target context; the autoregressive target then verifies proposed tokens for speculative decoding. Strongest baseline: The paper compares autoregressive target decoding with EAGLE-3 speculative decoding using 16- and 60-token draft-tree settings under its reported hardware and task setup. These are author-run comparisons; external tuning parity was not checked. Regime: Paper evaluations include Qwen3 4B/8B and Qwen3 Coder 30B-A3B plus Llama-3.1 8B Instruct, math/code/chat tasks, maximum 2048 generated tokens in Table 1, and NVIDIA H200 GPUs unless noted. Additional SGLang/vLLM serving and long-context results are reported in separate sections/appendix. Limitations: Reported evaluations use selected models, datasets, decoding settings and NVIDIA H200 hardware; latency and throughput gains may change with hardware, batch size, concurrency, prompt/output lengths and serving configuration.; Comparisons depend on draft/block size and method-specific tuning. The paper reports the largest differences against selected EAGLE-3 configurations; this is not a universal comparison across all speculative-decoding methods or workloads.; The results are author-run. Public code and checkpoints are linked, but this activation did not install, execute or independently reproduce them.; The repository currently documents additional model and framework integrations, including DFlash 2; those later integrations are distinct from the paper's evaluated results and were not tested. Contrary evidence: Within the paper's own task table, speedups vary: MT-Bench is lower than the math and code workloads, and gains decrease at temperature 1. The result supports workload-dependent acceleration rather than one fixed speedup.; EAGLE-3's speedup rises when its draft tree is expanded from 16 to 60 tokens, narrowing the comparison on several rows; speedup depends on comparison budget and tuning. Open evidence gaps: No independent reproduction of speed, output equivalence or resource use was found in this review.; Transfer to different accelerator generations, high-concurrency production serving, long-context workloads and total fleet cost is not established by the inspected results. Sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.06036v2 · https://github.com/z-lab/dflash 4. LIMBO learns a humanoid safety boundary and distills it into a task policy Desk: agents_memory Evidence: A · credible_unconfirmed · active · importance 6/10 (Major) Importance rationale: If reproduced and extended, synthesizing a state-action safety value from black-box transitions and distilling it into a humanoid task policy could reduce dependence on hand-designed barriers and runtime filters. The preprint reports a 29-DoF simulation-to-hardware study, but hardware samples are small, one human-throw comparison is not statistically significant, and the learned approximation is not a general safety guarantee. What changed: Gonzales et al. introduce LIMBO, which learns a state-action control barrier value from black-box transitions around a frozen base controller, then uses it as a teacher to train a task policy that can run without an online safety filter. Their arXiv paper reports simulation and hardware experiments on a 29-degree-of-freedom humanoid performing dodgeball avoidance and locomotion beneath low obstacles. In human-thrown dodgeball trials, the distilled policy evaded 20 of 26 throws versus 18 of 26 for an analytical-barrier baseline; the paper says this hit-rate difference is not statistically significant. For repeated synthetic trajectories, both methods had a 10.2% hit rate, while the distilled policy showed lower drift and tilt. These are author-reported results from one preprint, not a broad safety guarantee or independent reproduction. Why it matters: LIMBO offers a concrete route from learned safety boundaries to policies that retain safety behavior at execution time without an online filter. The hardware demonstrations make the method relevant to whole-body robotics, while the small human-throw sample, limited tasks and learned approximation constrain what can be inferred about safety outside the tested regimes. Demonstrated: The preprint reports the method and its own simulation and hardware results. No independent hardware reproduction was performed in this review; broad safety of the learned approximation is not demonstrated. Claimed: In 26 human-thrown hardware trials, QCBF-PD evaded 20/26 throws versus 18/26 for CBF-RL; the paper says the hit-rate difference is not statistically significant. In 59 repeated synthetic hardware trajectories both methods had 10.2% hit rate, while QCBF-PD had lower median drift (0.162 vs 0.944 m) and tilt (14.9° vs 32.4°). Mechanism: A residual-action Q-CBF is learned from black-box transitions and a state-based failure margin around a frozen stabilizing controller. Risk-guided replay concentrates data near the estimated recoverability boundary. The learned value then supplies action-level feedback and counterfactual corrections while training a task policy; the policy is deployed without an online safety filter. Strongest baseline: An analytical control-barrier-function reinforcement-learning controller (CBF-RL) and the frozen base controller; comparisons use the paper’s stated throw and synthetic-trajectory regimes. Regime: One 29-DoF humanoid; simulation training; two behaviors (dodgeball avoidance and low-obstacle locomotion); hardware tests include 26 human throws per controller and 59 identical scripted trajectories. Limitations: All empirical results are reported by one preprint and were not independently reproduced in this review.; The human-throw hardware comparison uses 26 throws per controller and its hit-rate difference is reported as not statistically significant.; The synthetic trajectory comparison uses 59 repeated trajectories and has the same hit rate for both controllers; improvements are reported in drift and tilt.; The results cover dodgeball avoidance and low-obstacle locomotion on one 29-DoF humanoid; they do not establish broad task or hardware transfer.; The formal viability result assumes a specified state-based safety margin and system regularity; the learned discounted Q-CBF is an approximation, not proof that a deployed policy is safe in arbitrary conditions. Open evidence gaps: The reported hardware results have not been independently reproduced, and the human-throw comparison is small and not statistically significant for hit rate.; The paper does not establish that the learned Q-CBF approximation or distilled policy preserves safety under untested dynamics, failures or task specifications. Sources: https://arxiv.org/html/2609.22075 5. PIR reads answers that language models conceal in internal activations Desk: agents_memory Evidence: A · credible_unconfirmed · active · importance 6/10 (Major) Importance rationale: If independently validated, a reference-free readout that distinguishes concealed answers from unknown items could strengthen audits of sandbagging and unlearning, where output-only evaluation is ambiguous. The paper reports results across several open-model families and concealment setups, but uses author-run organisms, has limited external validation, and explicitly demonstrates an adversarially trained model that defeats the probe. What changed: Dingeto introduces Probe of Internal Recognition (PIR), which contrasts candidate-answer activations to read which answer a language model internally recognizes, even when its output differs. The author reports balanced answer-decoding accuracy of 0.70–0.87 across eight models from five families, versus 0.28–0.40 unknown-item baselines, and reports that the signal remains high under several tested forms of concealment. The paper also reports a deployment detector AUC of 0.718 on a trained sandbagger and distinguishes some unlearning runs from concealment. Limits are material: an adversarially trained anti-probe model drives the readout to baseline while retaining capability; the deployment detector needs the model’s base checkpoint; open-ended reasoning without enumerable answers is outside scope; and several experiments are single-seed author runs. These are preprint results, not independent confirmation of a reliable safety monitor. Why it matters: Capability evaluations can confuse a model that hides an answer with one that does not know it. PIR proposes a white-box signal for that distinction and tests it against several concealment and unlearning setups. Its demonstrated evasion case and checkpoint requirements make it a possible audit component for a defined threat model, not a general lie detector or standalone safety guarantee. Demonstrated: The inspected v2 preprint describes the method, experiments and an anti-probe evasion result. No independent reproduction was performed; the results do not establish a general safety monitor. Claimed: Under prompted concealment, the author reports balanced recognition accuracy of 0.70–0.87 across eight models from five families versus unknown-item baselines of 0.28–0.40. The deployment detector reaches AUC 0.718 on one trained sandbagger; external-organism and free-form results differ by setup. Mechanism: For each question, PIR contrasts activation spans of the correct candidate and distractors to form a recognition direction, then decodes the highest-scoring candidate. A deployment divergence detector compares the readout with the model output. The detector is calibrated using the model’s own base checkpoint; a separately trusted honest model is not required. Strongest baseline: Unknown-item recognition baseline and, for deployment detection, text-only and black-box behavioral detectors on the same stated question splits. Regime: Eight models across five open-model families; MMLU, WMDP, ARC-Challenge and TriviaQA; prompted and trained concealment, external password-locked/circuit-broken models and selected unlearning checkpoints. Limitations: All empirical results are reported in one preprint; no independent reproduction was performed in this review.; An adversarially trained anti-probe organism defeats both tested monitors while retaining capability, so robustness applies only when models are not trained to evade the readout.; The deployment divergence detector requires access to the model’s own base or honest checkpoint and is not a fully black-box monitor.; The method requires candidate answers and does not cover open-ended reasoning for which answers cannot be enumerated.; Several author-created organisms use single seeds; external validation covers only selected concealment types, and the free-form detector is shown on one model and factual questions.; The strict rotation-consistency gate selects which questions count as known; the clean domain-specific erasure result relies on one author-run RMU experiment. Open evidence gaps: The paper’s multi-model recognition and concealment results have not been independently reproduced, and several author-created organisms use single seeds.; The anti-probe experiment shows an optimized adversary can defeat both tested monitors; robustness against adaptive evasion is not established. Sources: https://arxiv.org/html/2609.21996v2 6. SeeQ reports subtask-value steering gains on four real-world bimanual robot tasks Desk: evaluation_science Evidence: A · credible_unconfirmed · active · importance 6/10 (Major) Importance rationale: If the reported steering gains generalize, subtask-level value learning could make large, imperfect robot datasets more useful for improving long-horizon manipulation and provide a practical critic layer around generalist policies. That could change robotics training and deployment choices, but current evidence is limited to four tasks, 24 trials per task, target-task fine-tuning and one author-reported paper; it is a major engineering direction, not a confirmed broad capability shift. What changed: A September 2026 Carnegie Mellon preprint introduces SeeQ, a generalist 3B value model for steering robot policies on long-horizon bimanual manipulation. It predicts the active subtask in language, estimates action values over that shorter horizon, then selects among 8 candidate action chunks proposed by a separate base policy. Across four real-robot tasks on two platforms, the authors report that SeeQ steering raises success from 10/24 to 22/24 for shirt hanging, 10/24 to 15/24 for lid sealing, 9/24 to 17/24 for grocery packing, and 5/24 to 10/24 for LEGO disassembly. A RoboCOIN-pretrained checkpoint is publicly listed, but the authors fine-tune it on each target task; its values are not calibrated task-success probabilities. The small trials have not been independently reproduced, and subtask prediction errors or locally helpful actions that harm later stages remain limitations. Why it matters: If reproduced, learning action values over the current subtask could make broad robot datasets more useful for steering generalist policies through long tasks without propagating sparse final-success reward across the entire trajectory. The results make this a concrete, artifact-backed research direction for value learning in robotics, while the small number of trials and task-specific fine-tuning limit claims of general transfer. Claimed: The authors report that best-of-8 SeeQ steering increased base-policy success on four real bimanual tasks: shirt hanging 10/24 to 22/24; lid sealing 10/24 to 15/24; grocery packing 9/24 to 17/24; LEGO disassembly 5/24 to 10/24. The paper reports a mean increase from 35.4% to 66.7% across these tasks. Mechanism: A 3B PaliGemma-based Q-function is pretrained on annotated, diverse bimanual robot data. It autoregressively predicts the currently active subtask in natural language, then estimates the value of candidate action chunks for completing that subtask. Training uses subtask-level temporal-difference targets that stop at subtask boundaries and a best-of-8 backup from a generalist base policy. At inference, the critic ranks action chunks proposed by that separate policy. Strongest baseline: Same base policy without value steering; for two tasks, same PaliGemma backbone and matching pretraining/task data with task-level Monte Carlo, task-level TD, and subtask-level SARSA objectives. All comparisons use 24 trials per method/task. Regime: 3B PaliGemma-based Q-function pretrained on the bimanual portion of RoboCOIN (131 tasks, approximately 40,000 episodes, approximately 31.3 million steps); downstream fine-tuning on four real-world bimanual tasks, using xArm-7 or YAM platforms; 24 policy-steering trials per task; best-of-8 action selection from a fixed pi-0.5 base policy. Each task's finetuning data composition differs. Limitations: This is one author-reported preprint; no independent reproduction of the real-robot results was established in this review.; Each real-world task is evaluated over 24 trials. Trial counts are small, and the paper does not provide a multi-lab evaluation or establish robustness across broad object, scene or hardware distributions.; The generalist value model is fine-tuned on each target task before deployment; zero-shot transfer or performance with substantially less downstream data remains unestablished.; SeeQ scores action chunks proposed by a fixed base policy and cannot recover actions absent from that candidate set. Its model card says values are subtask-level returns, not calibrated probabilities of full-task success.; The authors note that subtask annotations can be ambiguous, subtask prediction errors can misdirect the critic, and local progress can make later subtasks harder even when current-subtask value rises.; The model card reports little improvement over the base policy on the simulation tasks they tested after fine-tuning; the authors attribute this to a mismatch between real-robot pretraining data and simulation, which remains a limited provider-side explanation. Open evidence gaps: No independent reproduction or larger repeated-trial study was established for the reported real-robot steering gains.; The work establishes per-task fine-tuned steering, not broad zero-shot transfer or performance with minimal downstream data.; Subtask-local values may conflict with downstream task success, and incorrect subtask prediction can cause the critic to rank actions against the wrong objective. Sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22085 · https://huggingface.co/CMU-AIRe/SeeQ-3B 7. Apple-affiliated preprint reports one compact vision-language model family across digital-agent tasks Desk: agents_memory Evidence: A · credible_unconfirmed · active · importance 6/10 (Major) Importance rationale: If the reported integration holds under matched independent evaluation, one 2B–8B model family covering several digital-agent capabilities could change model selection and deployment design, while the training system could broaden how interactive agents are post-trained. This is a major engineering direction, but the result is one author-reported preprint with no independent reproduction or public artifact located here, so confidence and transfer remain limited. What changed: An Apple-affiliated September 2026 preprint describes MintAct, a family of 2B, 4B and 8B vision-language models trained to combine screenshot-based UI grounding, multi-step mobile/desktop/web navigation and visual tool use. The authors use staged supervised learning, per-domain reinforcement-learning specialists distilled into one model, and asynchronous online RL with an explicitly controlled training mix. They report MintAct-8B scores of 48.9 on OSWorld-Verified, 74.7 on Weblica, 67.0 on AndroidWorld and 24.5 on MM-ToolSandBox, with many size-matched specialist comparisons favorable but not uniformly so. These are author-reported benchmark results without independent reproduction. The final joint-RL experiment covers mobile and desktop rather than all domains; the authors leave all-domain joint RL for future work, and no public model or code release was located in this review. Why it matters: If reproduced, a compact model family that combines grounding, cross-device navigation and tool use could reduce the need to train and serve separate specialist agents. The paper also shows how asynchronous environment infrastructure and explicit domain balancing address a systems bottleneck in interactive-agent training. The evidence does not establish open availability, deployment reliability, or a cost advantage over specialists. Claimed: The authors report that 2B/4B/8B MintAct models combine UI grounding, mobile/desktop/web navigation and visual tool use while matching or exceeding many similarly sized specialists on their stated benchmarks. MintAct-8B reports 48.9 on OSWorld-Verified, 74.7 on Weblica, 67.0 on AndroidWorld and 24.5 on MM-ToolSandBox. Mechanism: A staged recipe builds high-resolution grounding and multi-step supervised skills, trains reinforcement-learning specialists per domain and distills them into a single model, then performs asynchronous agentic RL with a target sampling distribution across heterogeneous environments. Domain-specific prompts select the relevant action space while a shared screenshot/coordinate interface supports transfer. Strongest baseline: Within each benchmark, the paper compares against its Qwen3-VL initialization and listed size-matched public or per-domain specialist models; the authors also compare joint SFT/RL against per-domain specialist training in ablations. Cross-paper comparisons are not uniformly matched experiments. Regime: Apple-affiliated preprint submitted 18 September 2026; 2B, 4B and 8B model sizes initialized from Qwen3-VL variants; grounding, Android mobile, Linux desktop, local/replayed web and MM-ToolSandBox visual-tool environments; benchmark protocols and task limits vary by benchmark. Final joint-RL runs mix mobile and desktop, with reported web transfer; visual tool use is excluded from that joint-RL stage. Limitations: This is one author-reported preprint; no independent reproduction, model-card audit or deployment evaluation was established in this review.; The arXiv record did not link public code or checkpoints during this review. Training data, full infrastructure and production serving details were not independently inspected.; Many benchmark baselines are drawn from papers with different evaluation setups; performance should be compared only within each stated benchmark and protocol. Some MintAct scores do not exceed the best listed specialist or public model.; The final joint reinforcement-learning experiment covers mobile and desktop, not web and visual tool use together. Reported transfer from mobile/desktop to web is bounded to the tested setup; joint RL across all domains is left for future work.; The authors report synthetic environments can help where real interaction data are scarce, but real in-domain RL performs better where real data are available; no general cost, quality-adjusted throughput or production economics advantage is established.; Benchmark scores do not establish reliable completion on arbitrary live interfaces, authorization safety, real-user utility, or on-device performance. Open evidence gaps: Reported cross-domain results have not been independently reproduced under matched benchmark protocols; no public checkpoint/code was located during review.; The paper argues one family can match specialists, but some comparison rows come from separate papers and differing protocols, and a single joint-RL model was not trained across all four domains.; The paper does not establish the economic or operational tradeoff between unified training/serving, per-domain specialists, and synthetic versus real environment training. Sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22083 8. A preprint formalizes how to verify revocation across long-running agent work Desk: agents_memory Evidence: A · credible_unconfirmed · active · importance 6/10 (Major) Importance rationale: If implemented across real providers, a bounded certificate that accounts for delegated and in-flight work could materially improve how agent systems revoke authority and prevent late external effects. The result is an author-proposed protocol with a local provider-free evaluation, not evidence of deployment or broad adoption. What changed: A September 18 preprint defines root-scoped authorization quiescence for agents whose work can survive in queues, callbacks, delegated credentials and provider operations. It combines a durable root-epoch cut, sink-side fences, carrier accounting and provider evidence into a bounded certificate. The paper proves conditional safety properties and reports a provider-free 17-case late-effect suite plus a separately implemented checker; the results were not independently reproduced in this review. Why it matters: If the method holds under real provider adapters, it gives agent systems a more precise shutdown guarantee than cancellation acknowledgement or token revocation alone, while preserving work that has an independent authorization root. The paper explicitly limits its guarantee to registered, completely mediated paths, so it does not establish global idleness or real-world deployment safety. Claimed: The authors report 17/17 registered provider-free runner outcomes, 17/17 separate checker decisions and rejection of 44/44 semantically modified and consistently rehashed traces. The local protected sink rejects scheduled late effects under cut-plus-fence cases while cancellation-only and cut-only cases admit them. Mechanism: The protocol durably retires a root epoch, stops old-root authority expansion, installs operation-time fences at protected sinks, accounts for carriers and transfers, and composes provider-frontier leaf certificates into a cutset. Multi-root support uses antichains of minimal sufficient root sets; ongoing work can continue only through an exact rebind to a current witness independent of the retired root. Strongest baseline: The paper compares cancellation acknowledgement alone and root cut without sink fencing against the same scheduled unit and local protected-effect oracle under cut-plus-fence. Its cited RISU v0.3 artifact is a complementary fixed-profile evidence verifier, not an active protocol or provider integration; no matched tests against remote provider implementations are reported. Regime: Formal claims apply to registered endpoints and protected sinks whose authority lineage, carriers and cross-provider transfers are completely mediated or conservatively represented. The executed suite uses a provider-free local ledger, child worker processes, logical endpoint shapes and inert typed effects. Limitations: All formal and evaluation claims are reported by the paper authors; the proof and artifact were not independently audited or reproduced here.; The test suite is provider-free and uses a local protected sink; endpoint labels do not establish actual MCP, A2A, OAuth, scheduler or cloud-provider behavior.; The guarantee is relative to a retired authorization root and complete bounded manifest; it does not mean global idleness, rollback, business completion or physical cessation.; Correctness depends on complete mediation/accounting, sound sink fences and exact cross-provider channel conservation; opaque endpoints may leave the result indeterminate.; The paper’s cited RISU Bounded Agent Closure v0.3 specification was inspected and appears complementary in scope: it verifies submitted evidence for a fixed profile but expressly has no actuators, integrations, orchestration or distributed protocol. Neither source establishes a deployed end-to-end provider implementation. Open evidence gaps: No independent execution of the proof checker or registered late-effect suite was performed.; No implementation or test evidence was inspected for actual remote provider adapters or production agent runtimes.; The paper cites RISU Bounded Agent Closure v0.3, whose Phase-1 specification verifies submitted closure evidence for a fixed profile and explicitly excludes actuators, integrations, orchestration and distributed protocols; the paper presents its active cut/fencing protocol as complementary. No comparison with a deployed orchestration system or actual provider adapter was performed. Sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.21284 · https://github.com/risu-research/bounded-agent-closure/blob/a46456f028cd3dd1d386111b1faab890a26ae5e9/SPEC.md 9. TierKV combines predictive KV-cache compression and flash tiers for mobile LLM inference Desk: inference_systems Evidence: A · credible_unconfirmed · active · importance 6/10 (Major) Importance rationale: If replicated across representative mobile workloads, reducing KV-cache memory while preserving long-context access could materially expand on-device inference capability and privacy-preserving deployment. The reported results are bounded to the tested models and SoCs, with baseline-dependent speedups and no independent implementation audit. What changed: Shu et al. describe TierKV, an accepted EuroSys 2027 system that predicts cache demand from prefill states and jointly places tokens in exact, low-rank and flash-offloaded tiers. In the authors’ eight-model, three-mobile-SoC evaluation, it reduced RAM-resident KV cache by 12.5–34% and improved prefill throughput by up to 17.6× versus MNN-LLM; the largest speedup is baseline-specific. Average end-to-end speedup was 1.10× versus llama.cpp, while decoding throughput fell in some cases from SVD reconstruction. These are paper-reported results; no independent reproduction was performed. Why it matters: On-device inference is constrained by shared memory and storage bandwidth. Jointly planning compression, cache residency and offload before decoding is a concrete systems approach to longer contexts under fixed device memory, but measured gains depend on the workload and comparator. Demonstrated: The accepted EuroSys 2027 paper (arXiv:2609.21172v2) and its method, platform, baselines, tables and accuracy/multi-turn results were inspected. Reported measurements were not independently reproduced. Claimed: The authors evaluate eight text, vision and audio models on three mobile SoCs. They report 12.5–34% lower resident KV-cache memory, up to 17.6× prefill throughput versus MNN-LLM in selected cases, and 1.10× average end-to-end speedup versus llama.cpp; SVD reconstruction reduces decoding throughput in some configurations. Mechanism: Before decoding, Predictive Multi-Tier Cache Optimization uses prefill hidden states to estimate sequence demand and jointly assigns cache tokens to exact, SVD-compressed resident and flash-offloaded tiers under memory and fidelity constraints. Strongest baseline: Three mobile inference frameworks are compared, but availability differs by model; MLC-LLM supports only a subset. The reported 17.6× maximum is against MNN-LLM, while the paper reports 1.10× average end-to-end speedup versus llama.cpp. Regime: Eight models across text, image and audio workloads on Adreno 740/750 and Mali-G715 mobile SoCs; OnePlus 12 end-to-end comparisons include llama.cpp, MNN-LLM and MLC-LLM where supported. Limitations: Author-reported system measurements; no independent implementation audit or reproduction was performed.; The maximum 17.6× prefill throughput comparison is against MNN-LLM on selected workloads; average end-to-end improvement over llama.cpp is 1.10×.; Comparisons are incomplete where baseline frameworks do not support the same model or long-context regime.; SVD reconstruction lowers decode throughput in some cases; prefill gains do not imply faster decoding in every workload.; Device results are limited to three evaluated mobile SoCs; thermal throttling and external validity remain concerns. Open evidence gaps: No independent reproduction of the system, speed, memory or accuracy measurements was conducted.; Cross-device generality and behavior under realistic prompt-length distributions, thermal throttling and competing storage/memory load remain uncertain. Sources: https://arxiv.org/html/2609.21172v2 10. A paper introduces a five-platform benchmark for hybrid computer-use agents and reports a large gap between aggregate scores and full behavioral tests Desk: agents_memory Evidence: A · credible_unconfirmed · active · importance 6/10 (Major) Importance rationale: If useful beyond the authors’ benchmark, a five-platform environment joining GUI operation, coding and execution-grounded verification could change how long-horizon computer-use agents are trained and evaluated. Its significance is major for this subfield, while benchmark representativeness and reported model results remain unreplicated. What changed: The authors introduce RecreationWorld, a framework for training and evaluating agents that alternate between exploring a running application through its interface, implementing a recreation in code, and executing it for feedback across Ubuntu, macOS, Windows, Android and Web. Their held-out RecreationBench has 250 tasks and reference-grounded hidden tests. In the authors’ evaluation of ten models, GPT-6 Astra scored 58.06% overall, but only 2.8% of tasks had a full programmatic pass; the paper reports that interface structure was reproduced more reliably than interactions and computed outputs. These are author-reported results from a new benchmark, not an independent capability comparison or a measure of general computer-use ability. Why it matters: Computer-use agents often need to combine interface exploration with code changes and then verify the running result. RecreationWorld offers a way to train that loop and score behavior against an executable reference. Its reported results also show why an aggregate score can overstate full behavioral fidelity: the leading model’s score was 58.06%, while full programmatic passes covered 2.8% of tasks in this benchmark. Independent replication and transfer beyond the authors’ task set remain open. Demonstrated: The inspected v2 paper contains the framework description, benchmark protocol and reported results. The release artifacts and model evaluations were not independently rerun here. Claimed: Authors report GPT-6 Astra achieved 58.06% aggregate score (Claude Opus 5 44.16%) and that GPT-6 Astra obtained full programmatic passes on tasks totaling 2.8% coverage. They report static structure was reproduced more reliably than interactions and computed outputs. Mechanism: Agents alternate GUI exploration, code implementation and execution/visual verification while reproducing an application from a running reference. Reference behavior supports hidden programmatic and visual assertions; the framework also uses generated trajectories for training. Strongest baseline: The reported model comparison includes ten frontier systems; GPT-6 Astra is compared with Claude Opus 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol under the paper’s benchmark configurations. This is not an independently matched evaluation across all inference stacks. Regime: Five-platform framework across Ubuntu, macOS, Windows, Android and Web; 250 held-out benchmark tasks; ten frontier models evaluated using the paper’s specified direct-MCP configurations. Limitations: Results are reported by the paper authors and were not independently reproduced in this activation.; RecreationBench comprises 250 reference-recreation tasks; its representativeness of real computer-use work and transfer to other task formulations remain uncertain.; The overall score is not equivalent to full task correctness; 2.8% full programmatic pass coverage for GPT-6 Astra is the paper’s reported value under its scoring protocol.; The benchmark compares the listed frontier models under paper-specific inference configurations; it does not establish general ranking across workloads, prompts, models or harnesses.; The reported association between broader exploration and stronger scores is descriptive and does not establish that exploration caused the performance difference. Open evidence gaps: No independent team has rerun RecreationBench or checked whether its hidden tests and scores generalize to other computer-use tasks.; Transfer beyond reference-recreation tasks, the five supported platforms and the paper’s model/harness configurations is not established. Sources: https://arxiv.org/html/2609.22000 11. SWE-Proof reports that machine-checkable specifications improve issue resolution, while specification faithfulness limits autonomous gains Desk: evaluation_science Evidence: A · credible_unconfirmed · active · importance 6/10 (Major) Importance rationale: If the reported benchmark results hold in this formal-methods regime, supplying a faithful machine-checkable specification can materially raise issue-resolution success and expose a class of defects hidden by tests. The work changes evaluation and verification design for repository agents, but self-generated specification synthesis remains weak and the result is not a general proof of autonomous software correctness. What changed: The v2 SWE-Proof paper builds a 500-issue benchmark from SWE-bench Verified and a Python subset of SWE-bench Pro, pairing each issue with a formal specification, a verifying implementation, and a ground-truth patch. On SWE-bench Verified, the authors report that a correctly supplied specification raised resolution from an 85% unaided baseline to about 95%, while adding verification to an end-to-end agent that writes its own specification did not improve its roughly 85% baseline. In a separate specification-synthesis test, only 56% of model-written specifications passed the paper’s five-property audit; incomplete behavioral coverage (faithfulness) was the main failure. The results are author-reported. Their guarantee depends on audited axioms and faithful refinement from verified code to the executed patch, and the audit panel itself uses language models. Why it matters: The paper separates proof checking from the harder task of expressing the intended behavior faithfully. Its reported gap suggests formal verification can catch defects missed by tests when the specification is sound, while an agent that writes its own incomplete specification can gain little. This is consequential for software-agent evaluation and tool design, but does not show that general coding agents can autonomously produce correct proofs or specifications in ordinary repositories. Demonstrated: The v2 arXiv paper describes its 500-instance benchmark, verification pipeline, evaluation settings, audit procedures, reported outcomes and limitations. No independent rerun of the benchmark or inspection of the released proof bundles has been completed; all performance and trustworthiness results remain author-reported. Claimed: Authors report that hidden tests miss about one quarter of defects caught by verification, and that a correct supplied formal specification raises SWE-bench Verified resolution from an approximately 85% unaided baseline to approximately 95%. End-to-end agents writing their own specifications do not improve the baseline; the specification-synthesis setting reports 56% of specifications passing the five-property audit. Mechanism: Benchproofer constructs formal specifications, axiomatizes unchanged repository behavior, and admits benchmark instances only after mechanical checks and adversarial language-model audits. A candidate patch must refine an implementation that verifies against the specification. Strongest baseline: Within-paper SWE-bench Verified comparisons include an unaided baseline, an end-to-end setting where the agent writes a specification and patch, and a verified-from-spec setting where the specification is supplied. Appendix reports repeated runs for major settings. Regime: Repository issue resolution on SWE-bench Verified (500 issues) and the Python fragment of SWE-bench Pro. Evaluated models/verifiers and budgets vary by formal backend; headline 85-to-95 comparison is on SWE-bench Verified. Open evidence gaps: No independent recomputation of the benchmark outcomes, repeated-run variation or verification-vs-test comparison has been performed.; The authors’ axiom-soundness and refinement-fidelity evidence, including language-model audit panels, has not been independently red-teamed.; Transfer to other programming languages, repositories, issue distributions and verification backends is not established by the headline result. Sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.21190 · https://arxiv.org/html/2609.21190v2 12. A preprint reports measurable retention loss across multi-agent research handoffs Desk: evaluation_science Evidence: A · credible_unconfirmed · active · importance 6/10 (Major) Importance rationale: If the reported retention losses generalize, adding agent tiers could materially reduce how much useful research reaches decision makers, changing the expected value of multi-agent decomposition. The evidence is one author-reported paper and one research scaffold, so the consequence is conditional. What changed: A September 15 preprint models how multi-agent decomposition affects the findings that survive to a root agent. It derives a yield relationship under a stated retention model and reports measurements from 600 production deep-research traces and 16,082 tool-result handoffs. The empirical estimates are author-reported and tied to one research scaffold. Why it matters: If the measured loss generalizes, adding agent tiers can reduce the information that reaches a final decision maker, even when parallel agents surface more sources. The paper identifies a tradeoff between smaller working contexts and end-to-end retention that system designers can measure. Demonstrated: The paper and its method, reported measurements and limitations are publicly accessible. This activation did not reproduce the empirical measurements. Claimed: The authors report δ=0.34 (95% CI 0.30–0.38) from 600 production deep-research traces and C=0.571 (95% CI 0.527–0.615) across 16,082 tool-result hops; under their model, each added tier reduces yield. Mechanism: The paper models an agent handed b items as retaining each with probability r(b), composes this retention across a decomposition tree, and measures retention using production traces plus tool outputs with explicit item boundaries. Strongest baseline: Flat processing is the comparison for yield under the stated retention model; empirical C is measured at tool-result handoffs with explicit item boundaries. Regime: The empirical work covers the authors’ production deep-research traces and tool calls. The formal derivation applies under the paper’s stated retention assumptions. Limitations: All empirical findings are reported by the paper authors and were not independently reproduced in this activation.; The main trace corpus uses one research-agent scaffold; transfer to other systems or tasks is not established.; The analytical conclusion depends on the paper’s retention model and assumptions; it does not establish that flat systems are generally superior on total task quality, cost or latency. Open evidence gaps: No independent execution of the released scripts/corpora or replication of the reported constants was performed.; The empirical constants come from one research-agent scaffold; stability across other agents, task classes and tool boundaries is unmeasured. Sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.17464 Published edition · 2026-10-10

title: Research desk digest
summary: agents_memory LIMBO learns a humanoid safety boundary and distills it into a task policy — importance 6/10 · Gonzales et al. introduce LIMBO, which learns a state-action control barrier value from black-box transitions around a frozen base controller, then uses it as a teacher to train a task policy that can run without an online safety filter. Their arXiv paper reports simulation and hardware experiments on a 29-degree-of-freedom humanoid performing dodgeball avoidance and locomotion beneath low obstacles. In human-thrown dodgeball trials, the distilled policy evaded 20 of 26 throws versus 18 of 26 for an analytical-barrier baseline; the paper says this hit-rate difference is not statistically significant. For repeated synthetic trajectories, both methods had a 10.2% hit rate, while the distilled policy showed lower drift and tilt. These are author-reported results from one preprint, not a broad safety guarantee or independent reproduction. — FCMO-401B1D60C4E1 PIR reads answers that language models conceal in internal activations — importance 6/10 · Dingeto introduces Probe of Internal Recognition (PIR), which contrasts candidate-answer activations to read which answer a language model internally recognizes, even when its output differs. The author reports balanced answer-decoding accuracy of 0.70–0.87 across eight models from five families, versus 0.28–0.40 unknown-item baselines, and reports that the signal remains high under several tested forms of concealment. The paper also reports a deployment detector AUC of 0.718 on a trained sandbagger and distinguishes some unlearning runs from concealment. Limits are material: an adversarially trained anti-probe model drives the readout to baseline while retaining capability; the deployment detector needs the model’s base checkpoint; open-ended reasoning without enumerable answers is outside scope; and several experiments are single-seed author runs. These are preprint results, not independent confirmation of a reliable safety monitor. — FCMO-AC75B9BBD573 Apple-affiliated preprint reports one compact vision-language model family across digital-agent tasks — importance 6/10 · An Apple-affiliated September 2026 preprint describes MintAct, a family of 2B, 4B and 8B vision-language models trained to combine screenshot-based UI grounding, multi-step mobile/desktop/web navigation and visual tool use. The authors use staged supervised learning, per-domain reinforcement-learning specialists distilled into one model, and asynchronous online RL with an explicitly controlled training mix. They report MintAct-8B scores of 48.9 on OSWorld-Verified, 74.7 on Weblica, 67.0 on AndroidWorld and 24.5 on MM-ToolSandBox, with many size-matched specialist comparisons favorable but not uniformly so. These are author-reported benchmark results without independent reproduction. The final joint-RL experiment covers mobile and desktop rather than all domains; the authors leave all-domain joint RL for future work, and no public model or code release was located in this review. — FCMO-A10475EE549D A preprint formalizes how to verify revocation across long-running agent work — importance 6/10 · A September 18 preprint defines root-scoped authorization quiescence for agents whose work can survive in queues, callbacks, delegated credentials and provider operations. It combines a durable root-epoch cut, sink-side fences, carrier accounting and provider evidence into a bounded certificate. The paper proves conditional safety properties and reports a provider-free 17-case late-effect suite plus a separately implemented checker; the results were not independently reproduced in this review. — FCMO-6CE6ACBE9EDC A paper introduces a five-platform benchmark for hybrid computer-use agents and reports a large gap between aggregate scores and full behavioral tests — importance 6/10 · The authors introduce RecreationWorld, a framework for training and evaluating agents that alternate between exploring a running application through its interface, implementing a recreation in code, and executing it for feedback across Ubuntu, macOS, Windows, Android and Web. Their held-out RecreationBench has 250 tasks and reference-grounded hidden tests. In the authors’ evaluation of ten models, GPT-6 Astra scored 58.06% overall, but only 2.8% of tasks had a full programmatic pass; the paper reports that interface structure was reproduced more reliably than interactions and computed outputs. These are author-reported results from a new benchmark, not an independent capability comparison or a measure of general computer-use ability. — FCMO-62A5D9416CA6 Meta paper reports agentic experiment controls caught a false negative in a 37-day retrieval campaign — importance 5/10 · Meta authors describe EvoPilot, a human-gated agent workflow for experiments spanning asynchronous training, publishing, serving and evaluation systems. In one 37-day Video Deep Dive campaign, an initial autoresearch comparison appeared to show a 22-point offline hit-rate decline, but review found the control and treatment used different effective output depths. A matched comparison later reported a 3.20-point offline gain for enabling the interaction head, and a separate seven-day randomized online test reported a 0.66% relative increase in the product’s VDD slice of Good Search Result Rate for Retention. The operational analysis includes nine of twenty rounds with complete records; results are reported by the system’s authors and do not establish cross-organization performance. — FCMO-1D031029BCF0 Designer-RSI reports replay-gated procedural memory gains for graphic-design agents — importance 5/10 · A September 18, 2026 preprint introduces Designer-RSI, a method for adapting an agent through an external procedural skill library while leaving model weights fixed. In five reported rounds over 1,406 design briefs, the library grew from 76 seeded skills to 139. The authors report that widening the library and revising existing skills worked better together than either alone on 200 held-out briefs (58.5% versus 49.4% and 48.6% win rates against the no-skill agent; p=0.025). Results span three backbones and design benchmarks, but some individual metrics regress. The replay gate protects only the sampled cases; the user-derived prompts and full internal evaluation set are not public, and no independent reproduction or human preference study is reported. — FCMO-519FC6E8909F A preprint tests a lightweight trust gate for conflicting memories in language-model agents — importance 4/10 · An arXiv v1 preprint proposes the Memory Decision Layer, a zero-trained-parameter controller that evaluates retrieved memories before generation using relevance, reliability and task risk, then chooses whether to adopt or abstain. In benchmark experiments with constructed memory conflicts, the authors report lower hallucination rates than standard retrieval-augmented generation in tested settings, including zero hallucinations in the tested high-risk samples for several models. On one Gemma TruthfulQA comparison, MDL and standard RAG both had 4.8% overall hallucination, while high-risk rates were 0.0% and 11.9%, respectively. The paper reports about 0.14 ms added latency when embeddings are precomputed, but also residual active-action errors. These are single-team paper results, not independent confirmation or evidence of production performance. — FCMO-1A31056E0F2C A preprint reports that graph-structured skills improve agent benchmark results over a skill-optimization baseline — importance 4/10 · A September 18 arXiv preprint represents reusable agent skills as a directed graph of execution steps and context-dependent paths, then optimizes them with population-based mutation and crossover. Across five benchmarks, the authors report higher average success than SkillOpt in three model/harness settings: +4.01 percentage points for GPT-5.4-nano without a harness, +1.76 points for GPT-5.4 without a harness, and +1.33 points for GPT-5.4 with the Codex harness. Results average three optimization runs; GraphSkillEvo is best in 13 of 14 evaluated settings, but trails on GPT-5.4-nano LiveMath. The authors also report lower aggregate optimization-token counts for the two no-harness settings. These are single-preprint results, not independently reproduced. — FCMO-31AFDCAA5916 Google publishes ARTEMIS, an open-source agent for Android automation and testing — importance 4/10 · Google’s public ARTEMIS repository provides natural-language Android automation through a reactive Flash profile and a slower plan-and-verify Pro profile, with CLI, Python SDK and MCP integrations for coding environments. The project describes accessibility-tree and OCR targeting with visual fallbacks, execution traces and history summaries. Its README claims 99%+ task completion on AndroidWorld’s 100+ multi-step tasks, but gives no model/version, per-task scores, trial counts or independent evaluation; this remains a first-party claim. — FCMO-9FBEC3B75775 architectures_scaling A preprint separates abstention and noise filtering as two functions of attention gates — importance 5/10 · An arXiv v2 paper argues that softmax attention lacks two distinct functions: abstaining when no context item is useful and filtering interference within values it reads. The author specifies separate mechanisms and reports matched training comparisons from 10M to 350M parameters in which gating gains shift from mostly abstention at the smallest scale to filtering contributing about as much at the largest; the effects are largely additive. Interference-injection experiments and checks on pretrained models up to 20B are also reported. This is one author-team study; downstream capability gains, production impact and independent reproduction remain unestablished. — FCMO-A3F6EF5036B2 evaluation_science OpenProblemBench reports judge-assessed model progress on 82 unresolved mathematics and physics problems — importance 6/10 · OpenProblemBench tests seven model-execution configurations on 82 literature-grounded unresolved questions in mathematics and theoretical physics. Four evaluator models review each frozen solution against explicit proof or computational obligations and score solved, partial or unsolved progress. The paper reports a 14.02% evaluator-averaged solve rate for GPT-6-Astra and 2.44–7.01% for the other configurations; substantive partial progress is also counted. These are author-reported evaluator judgments, not domain-expert validation of discoveries. The authors identify evaluator error correlation, uneven problem coverage, single runs per condition and varying execution resources as limitations. — FCMO-4ED3DA0CBECF SeeQ reports subtask-value steering gains on four real-world bimanual robot tasks — importance 6/10 · A September 2026 Carnegie Mellon preprint introduces SeeQ, a generalist 3B value model for steering robot policies on long-horizon bimanual manipulation. It predicts the active subtask in language, estimates action values over that shorter horizon, then selects among 8 candidate action chunks proposed by a separate base policy. Across four real-robot tasks on two platforms, the authors report that SeeQ steering raises success from 10/24 to 22/24 for shirt hanging, 10/24 to 15/24 for lid sealing, 9/24 to 17/24 for grocery packing, and 5/24 to 10/24 for LEGO disassembly. A RoboCOIN-pretrained checkpoint is publicly listed, but the authors fine-tune it on each target task; its values are not calibrated task-success probabilities. The small trials have not been independently reproduced, and subtask prediction errors or locally helpful actions that harm later stages remain limitations. — FCMO-16D548A05BB2 SWE-Proof reports that machine-checkable specifications improve issue resolution, while specification faithfulness limits autonomous gains — importance 6/10 · The v2 SWE-Proof paper builds a 500-issue benchmark from SWE-bench Verified and a Python subset of SWE-bench Pro, pairing each issue with a formal specification, a verifying implementation, and a ground-truth patch. On SWE-bench Verified, the authors report that a correctly supplied specification raised resolution from an 85% unaided baseline to about 95%, while adding verification to an end-to-end agent that writes its own specification did not improve its roughly 85% baseline. In a separate specification-synthesis test, only 56% of model-written specifications passed the paper’s five-property audit; incomplete behavioral coverage (faithfulness) was the main failure. The results are author-reported. Their guarantee depends on audited axioms and faithful refinement from verified code to the executed patch, and the audit panel itself uses language models. — FCMO-0AFE5F204A4E A preprint reports measurable retention loss across multi-agent research handoffs — importance 6/10 · A September 15 preprint models how multi-agent decomposition affects the findings that survive to a root agent. It derives a yield relationship under a stated retention model and reports measurements from 600 production deep-research traces and 16,082 tool-result handoffs. The empirical estimates are author-reported and tied to one research scaffold. — FCMO-F9D95842D53F Language models use experimental records to predict research outcomes in fixed evaluations — importance 6/10 · In an October 8 preprint, Wang and colleagues report that language models prompted with records of prior experiments rank unseen research interventions more accurately in five fixed research environments and improve experiment selection in their evaluations. They also report gains in five multi-round OLMo3-100M simulations. The results are author-reported: some cross-environment uncertainty intervals include zero, transfer evidence is limited to autoregressive pretraining, and independent reproduction and deployed research value remain unestablished. — FCMO-3F64511BFDFD ODU-Bench reports contextual intent and false-trigger gaps in multimodal assistants — importance 5/10 · Chen et al. introduce ODU-Bench, a benchmark of 2,078 audio and audio-visual demand/no-demand scenes, and report results for 14 native multimodal models. In the paper’s reported evaluation, the best-scoring model recovers 44.7% of key information specifically requiring visual, acoustic or dialogue context; 11 of 14 models trigger on more than half of no-demand scenarios, and Gemini 3.1 Pro triggers on 40.6%. These are author-reported benchmark results, not independently reproduced estimates of real-world assistant behavior. — FCMO-890EF9C3566B A controlled study reports reduced diversity after training successive paper-review models on synthetic reviews — importance 5/10 · Ho, Liu and Huang train a Llama 3.1 8B reviewer on ICLR 2018–2023 reviews, use it to generate reviews for ICLR 2024 papers, then train four successors on mixtures containing 0%, 33%, 66% or 100% explicitly synthetic reviews. With other training settings held fixed, their paper reports that synthetic exposure compressed rating distributions and monotonically reduced same-paper and corpus-level semantic diversity in the tested one-step setup. This is a controlled author-reported experiment, not a measurement of real-world AI assistance in peer review: the official reviews may themselves include unobserved AI assistance, and the paper does not test whether the effect compounds over further generations. — FCMO-C5AB43D32F5F A paper reports that stronger next-turn metrics did not transfer to customer-support workflow success — importance 5/10 · Laskar et al. compare gold-history next-action scoring with closed-loop execution on generated multi-turn customer-support workflows. Across Qwen3 4B/14B and Gemma 3 4B/12B, their paper reports that supervised fine-tuning increased average text-turn success by 25.2 percentage points, while tool-turn gains were smaller; the best fine-tuned model completed 8 of 77 tool workflows and no model passed the holistic workflow judge. The result is limited to the authors’ task generator, proprietary workflow dataset, and tested models; it does not establish that turn-level metrics are generally useless. — FCMO-5C1279ADE812 APort Vault reports zero unauthorized transfers behind a deterministic payment authorization layer in a human-attack replay benchmark — importance 5/10 · In arXiv:2609.22076v1, APort’s author replays 4,371 human-written attacks from a live payment-agent capture-the-flag event against 14 models from eight labs, comparing model-only execution with a deterministic pre-action authorization check. Across restricted Levels 2–4, the paper reports 140 transfers to disallowed recipients in 76,842 model-only evaluations and none in 69,297 evaluations behind the layer; 105 versus zero also occurs on 68,970 matched model, prompt and track triples. The zero is bounded by 790 source sessions (session-clustered rule-of-three upper bound 0.38%). The result concerns one simulated payment tool and a locally implemented policy engine; the paper discloses a Level 4 confirmation-code mismatch that makes its measured layer stricter than the published policy pack. No inference to other tool domains, live deployment rates, or benign-task overblocking is supported. — FCMO-99C2914CBB6D A preprint reports graph-format sensitivity and an adaptive reasoning scaffold for graph algorithms — importance 5/10 · A September 10 preprint introduces GT Bench, a synthetic evaluation of 24 classical graph problems across four textual/structural representations, and reports that the best input representation varies with graph and task structure. Its Graph Theory Agent (GTA) adds learned representation selection and plan/decompose scaffolding around a frozen executor. On the paper’s reported Phi-4 setting, accuracy rises from 53.5% to 69.1% on the easy split and 33.0% to 41.5% on the hard split; the authors also report transfer to other executors and benchmarks. These are author-reported results, not independently reproduced here. The abstract says 44 task–structure settings while Appendix C describes 43 reported settings. — FCMO-487412BD250E inference_systems DFlash reports parallel diffusion drafting for multi-fold speculative decoding speedups — importance 6/10 · DFlash uses a small block-diffusion model to draft multiple tokens in parallel, conditioned on hidden features extracted from a frozen autoregressive target model and injected into the drafter's key/value cache. search_text: Research desk digest agents_memory LIMBO learns a humanoid safety boundary and distills it into a task policy — importance 6/10 · Gonzales et al. introduce LIMBO, which learns a state-action control barrier value from black-box transitions around a frozen base controller, then uses it as a teacher to train a task policy that can run without an online safety filter. In human-thrown dodgeball trials, the distilled policy evaded 20 of 26 throws versus 18 of 26 for an analytical-barrier baseline; the paper says this hit-rate difference is not statistically significant. For repeated synthetic trajectories, both methods had a 10.2% hit rate, while the distilled policy showed lower drift and tilt. These are author-reported results from one preprint, not a broad safety guarantee or independent reproduction. — FCMO-401B1D60C4E1 PIR reads answers that language models conceal in internal activations — importance 6/10 · Dingeto introduces Probe of Internal Recognition (PIR), which contrasts candidate-answer activations to read which answer a language model internally recognizes, even when its output differs. The author reports balanced answer-decoding accuracy of 0.70–0.87 across eight models from five families, versus 0.28–0.40 unknown-item baselines, and reports that the signal remains high under several tested forms of concealment. The paper also reports a deployment detector AUC of 0.718 on a trained sandbagger and distinguishes some unlearning runs from concealment. summary: Reviewed and promoted bounded author-reported ODU-Bench benchmark results after full-text methods, Table 3 and appendix inspection; authored es-419 and zh-Hans editions. Reviewed current TierKV v2 accepted paper and promoted bounded eight-model/three-SoC results with regime and baseline-specific limits; authored both native editions. Reconciled SoftBank final tranche using first-party Japanese and English releases; separated transaction/ownership reporting from unestablished compute and R&D effects; authored both native editions. Reviewed and persisted editorial materiality deferrals with claim-bounded reasons for LLM judge-panel effective size, CIBuzzBench, and recursive language models. Reconciled SoftBank duplicate alias to owner candidate and retained source access limitation. Reviewed six source-backed recent arXiv promotion candidates against the bounded-claim standard. Re-read GPU KernelBench full paper (879 evaluations, reported addressable-runtime range and correctness exceptions), checked DENSE v4/v5 for material changes, and preserved specific evidence gaps/next actions for AHRR, Coda, CodeMidas and TinyCeNN-LM. Read ANPD’s Portuguese consultation page and draft technical note §§5.5.3.1–5.5.3.5, recorded the proposed 2027–28 AI/data-protection agenda as a nonbinding policy development, and authored the same-day brief entry plus native editions. FCMO-6CE6ACBE9EDC: Read the full root-scoped authorization-quiescence paper and its provider-free test design, then compare its cited RISU v0.3 specification. Promoted a bounded author-reported account with assurance boundary and independent-reproduction/provider-integration gaps. FCMO-57688EE6F24B: Read the full official Chinese CPC Central Committee/State Council Opinion and NDRC interpretation. Promoted the adopted AI-for-science, AI-plus, compute/data, application-pilot and governance direction; no delivery or impact inferred. Authored and airlock-validated complete es-419 and zh-Hans editions. CAND-2026-10-04-816E0F33: Reopened primary abstract; deferred pending bounded SALM benchmark/device and performance regime. CAND-2026-10-04-6402811A: Reopened primary abstract; deferred pending model, baseline, benchmark construction and cost conditions. CAND-2026-10-04-3B723157: Reopened primary abstract; deferred pending abstention metric, sample, baseline and answer-quality tradeoff. CAND-2026-10-04-8FF05A0D: Reopened primary abstract and reconciled alias memory; deferred pending k, compute and task-sample scope. CAND-2026-10-04-C00F0F4E: Rechecked Qwen official repository; retained duplicate disposition to the existing owner because the source does not support the intake hardware-standard claim. CAND-2026-10-04-084D9C98: Promoted after full-paper inspection; updated after prior-art specification comparison. Candidate records the source trail and concrete next tests. CAND-2026-10-09-3C8DF6AB: Accepted the recent official policy source after reading NDRC follow-up Q&A; separated adopted directions from implementation evidence. Priority review and promotion of the World Modeling in Transformers and GraphSkillEvo preprints, with full source inspection, matched-regime and limitation analysis; GraphSkillEvo author repository README reviewed, code not run. Priority review and promotion of the Memory Decision Layer preprint and the v2 abstention/noise-filtering attention study; paper-reported outcomes preserved with constructed benchmark, sample and reproduction limits. Reviewed the Commission C(2026)3472 final text for a common data-centre sustainability rating scheme; recorded design and left Official Journal/legal-effect and implementation status open. Rechecked the Oct 9 Anthropic report, Oct 9 FIBS paper and Brazil ANPD agenda in Portuguese against existing canonical records; updated review notes and candidate state where warranted. No new event qualified for the front page. Updated the Oct 10 historical edition with the completed depth reviews; kept the two-story front page because older-event promotions did not improve the recency frontier. Completed a partial ~36-hour high-velocity primary-source sweep across lab newsrooms/model releases, arXiv cs.AI/cs.CL/cs.LG listings and official policy pages. No distinct fresh material item meeting the editorial standard was found; Anthropic Oct 9 report was already canonical. Search/index and interval coverage remain partial. Reviewed source-backed queue candidates: duplicate-linked the September Anthropic cyber report to its existing canonical owner; promoted Designer-RSI (FCMO-519FC6E8909F), MintAct (FCMO-A10475EE549D), SeeQ (FCMO-16D548A05BB2), LIMBO (FCMO-401B1D60C4E1), and PIR (FCMO-AC75B9BBD573) after primary-source inspection; preserved author-reported status, limitations and open reproduction/evasion gaps. Re-read the official Chinese Jiangsu token/compute, corpus/data and model voucher notice and compared its written terms with the earlier Hangzhou Binjiang policy; refreshed the existing canonical record and source attribution. No budgets, awards, payments, uptake or economic effects were verified. Deep-read PIR anti-probe appendix and compared it with Anthropic’s primary report on cross-category failure of fine-tuned behavioral lie detectors. These are adjacent methods, not direct contradictory measurements; common held-out evaluation remains open. Read arXiv:2609.20974v1 full HTML, sections 3–6 and result tables; promoted bounded author-reported AAR results with retrieval and materialization limits; checked current arXiv history again and found only v1/no linked code. Read arXiv:2609.21257v1 §§3–6 and empirical tables; promoted a scoped EvoPilot case separating the online randomized effect from the operational system account and recording incomplete denominator/reproduction limits. Inspected the Portuguese ANPD Oct 9 release and selected sections of its 38-page second-cycle sandbox report; recorded three-pilot scope and inconclusive/incomplete test findings. Re-read Meta’s original Muse announcement and reconciled the same-event alias to the existing canonical owner; retained first-party-control versus independently measured security distinction. Read arXiv:2602.06036v2 method, benchmark table, serving/ablation sections and linked repository; promoted bounded author-reported speed results with workload, baseline and hardware limitations. Enumerated Oct 9 arXiv new-submission listings for cs.AI/cs.CL/cs.LG and sampled lead entries; full-read OpenProblemBench v1 §§3–6, results, judge sensitivity and limitations; promoted model-judged benchmark findings without treating them as verified discoveries. Checked original Chinese government policy surfaces; confirmed the Oct 9 CPC Central Committee/State Council Opinion was already represented canonically and found no distinct new event. Refreshed deterministic unpublished Oct 10 daily edition preview; no publication transaction or checkpoint advance.
