search_text: Research desk digest agents_memory Large Knowledge Model reports source-linked reasoning graphs and scientific retrieval gains — importance 6/10 · A September 2026 preprint describes a scientific retrieval system that stores paper-level claims, premises, reasoning chains, conditions and source links, then connects them into question, workflow and evidence views. The authors report nearly twice as many known supporting and contradicting evidence pairs retrieved on SciFact-Open, a 5-point citation-F1 improvement from adding reasoning graphs over the same retrieved papers, and gains on three fixed-model scientific QA benchmarks. The reported evaluations are author-run; omission errors, independent reproduction and direct evaluation of the landscape’s evidence categorization remain open. — FCMO-407911970824 ScholarStack reports cross-task reuse of layered scientific research assets — importance 6/10 · A September 2026 preprint describes a research-asset framework that keeps source-grounded paper statements, domain organization and scoped cross-paper syntheses as distinct but linked objects. Across four task families, the authors report that gains concentrate on multi-paper evidence tasks and that query-time token use falls where measured. On a 797-question multi-paper QA set, the paper reports a higher five-dimension score than its full-text baseline while using fewer generation tokens. Construction and judging costs are excluded from that comparison; results are author-reported and rely on benchmark- and judge-specific methods. — FCMO-ED6526B13300 A controlled agent-population study finds indirect convention shifts can lower tipping thresholds — importance 6/10 · A September 21 preprint studies how committed minorities can redirect conventions in homogeneous, fully connected naming-game populations of four open-weight LLMs. The authors report that fewer than 10% of single-intermediate paths reduce total committed effort versus a direct transition. In evaluated triplets, allowing a third convention during a single stage produces cost-effective transitions in 15–40% of cases across model populations, compared with 12–23% for isolated two-stage routes. These are results from a controlled model, not observed attacks or evidence about deployed heterogeneous agent networks. — FCMO-967377164E87 Alignment Inertia measures when system prompts and LoRA fail to override prior behavior — importance 5/10 · The Alignment Inertia preprint measures whether system prompts and LoRA fine-tuning override each model’s observed policy behavior on cases where that behavior conflicts with a target policy. It evaluates Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 on medical-misinformation and hate-speech datasets. Zero-shot prompting leaves some conflicting cases unresolved, with results varying by model, domain and policy direction; LoRA sometimes improves and sometimes worsens override success. These are author-reported behavioral results conditional on the study’s constructed divergence zones and adaptation data, not a universal measure of prompt or fine-tuning reliability. — FCMO-8FADF99E8A28 Paper reports pre-action memory signals and selective evidence retrieval for long-horizon agents — importance 5/10 · The PaMER paper studies whether an agent’s hidden state contains signals that predict when to compress context or retrieve older evidence. It proposes state-guided compression and selective raw-evidence retrieval. On the authors’ 260-task WorkBuddyBench evaluation with DeepSeek-V4-Flash, PaMER reduced mean total input/output tokens by 73.2% while mean task reward changed from 69.9 to 69.4; PaMER+ reduced tokens by 71.7% and raised mean reward to 71.6. These results are author-reported and specific to the benchmark, harness and model configuration. — FCMO-EFA0808F5D89 Paper reports claim-level workflow for multilingual continual document updates — importance 5/10 · The Knowledge Pull Requests (KPR) paper proposes an update workflow that extracts claims from new sources, classifies and routes them to document sections, flags conflicts, and records a claim-level changelog alongside the text diff. On cross-lingual Wikipedia revision and three constructed RAGTIME update settings, the authors report better information integration and retention than raw-text rewriting, claim-only rewriting, and scratch regeneration in the evaluated conditions. Their QA evaluation reports that KPR-edited articles provide a stronger grounding source than the original article, closed-book answers, or web search in cases where relevant knowledge appears only in other-language sources. — FCMO-53464968F2F9 Anthropic preprint reports AI-assisted discovery of repeat-associated phage reverse transcriptases — importance 5/10 · Anthropic’s September 23 preprint describes an autonomous genome-mining campaign in which Claude agents searched reverse-transcriptase loci across 1.9 billion metagenomic protein clusters and surfaced array-associated reverse transcriptases (ART), a candidate family of phage RT loci with tandem non-coding DNA repeats and neighboring partner genes. The authors report 95 ART RT representatives and experiments detecting distinct short RNAs from arrays during phage infection and plasmid expression. These are provider-authored paper results, not an independent replication. The preprint says repeated reruns missed the array and explicitly leaves RT activity, RNA substrate use, partner interaction and phage function unknown. The result supports a bounded claim that an AI-agent campaign surfaced a biologically investigated candidate system; it does not establish a functional CRISPR-like enzyme or a general autonomous-discovery rate. — FCMO-E8FC79A21E00 Source-aligned agent-memory units improve complete-evidence retrieval in a synthetic trace benchmark — importance 5/10 · A paper introduces Execution Provenance Graph Memory (EPGM) for retrieving complete supporting evidence from long agent execution histories under a fixed token budget. On 2,000 queries over 1,207 held-out ISETrace trajectories, the authors report that source-aligned provenance units improve Full Support@2048 by 19.07 points over flat 512-token windows and by 11.96 points over a per-metric oracle across four flat chunk sizes, with matched Dense-FT scoring. Holding candidate units and seed scores fixed, a graph-conditioned residual adds a smaller 4.55 points (95% CI 2.98–6.18), concentrated on queries whose evidence spans multiple events. The corpus is synthetic and the results are author-reported; no independent reproduction was performed. — FCMO-71A18CEA363D EDGEGEN reports gains from specification-derived edge-case tasks for tool-calling agents — importance 5/10 · EDGEGEN extracts compliance rules from an agent specification, combines structured rule-violation scenarios with executable database states, and uses the generated tasks for fine-tuning or harness optimization. The authors report improvement over the base model in all 18 model–benchmark comparisons across three benchmarks; on tau2-bench Airline they report relative mean-progress gains ranging from 2% to 42%, while one harness-optimization result for Gemma-4-e4b is 10% above human-curated and 30% above the base harness. Main evaluations use only 10–15 scenarios per benchmark. In a small audit, human reviewers confirmed only 6 of 10 Airline and 4 of 10 ToolSandbox runs labeled successful. These are preprint-reported results, not independently reproduced evidence of general agent reliability. — FCMO-89DF6E8A7BC3 EvoOntology reports gains from queryable semantic state and a regression-blocking evolution gate — importance 5/10 · EvoOntology presents an MCP-served ontology that data agents can query at runtime and refine through typed edits admitted only after paired evaluation on held-out tasks. On three data-agent benchmarks, the authors report improvements over no-ontology baselines across multiple backbones. On DDR-Bench, the paper reports a mean Trajectory-Wise gain of 12.3 percentage points from the initial ontology and another 7.7 points after self-evolution; on BIRD, initial ontology improves execution accuracy by 5.1 points and evolution adds 3.7. In an ablation averaged across four backbones, removing the paired gate lowers the final DDR-Bench score from 89.5 to 78.3 (-11.2 points), the largest drop among four loop components. These are author-reported results from a single preprint; no independent reproduction is reported here. — FCMO-17E52DF2A714 EmbodiedMemory-Bench reports simulation results for action-outcome memory — importance 4/10 · The EmbodiedMemory-Bench preprint evaluates memory methods over 2,554 interactive episodes in four embodied-task families. The authors report matched-backbone comparisons for external action-outcome memory and show that adding maximal historical RGB context can reduce Gemini-3-Flash average success by 10.4 percentage points in the reported comparison. The paper does not establish physical-robot performance, independent reproduction or deployment benefit. — FCMO-404D6DE57426 COMPASS reports decentralized language-model control for 1,024-agent flocking rollouts — importance 4/10 · A robotics preprint presents COMPASS, which couples per-agent language-model reasoning states to a learned multi-agent spatial transformer (MAST) that exchanges local neighbor messages and generates both low-level actions and a feedback token. In a matched-retained-count offline analysis, authors report next-action Top-3 block retention of 0.69 versus 0.31 for geometry-only selection across 650 checkpoints from 32 trajectories, while pooled centroid similarity rounds to 0.98 in both conditions. Across ALFWorld, WebShop and tau2-bench, the authors report gains over memory baselines, including 16.2 and 16.3 percentage-point success-rate gains over the strongest same-block learned write-time baseline on ALFWorld and WebShop. The authors call this “early posterior collapse” and measure “old-hypothesis contamination” in final outputs. Across 7,160 trials using Gemini-2.5-Pro and Gemini-2.5-Flash, ambiguous-first dialogues performed worse than clarified-first dialogues despite equivalent final task-relevant information. On a reported 64-xPU 3D-mesh testbed, the authors report lower communication latency and higher bandwidth than their RoCE comparison system, plus faster DeepSeek R1 inference. Its accounting examples include synthetic billing fixtures: in one constructed deployment, owner labels only on leader pods left 66% of GPU spend unowned, while a fallback assigned 61% to a Helm chart label. These results show that labels, source overlap and allocation rules can change reported cost ownership, not that they change total compute expense or establish a uniquely correct cost split. — FCMO-495193A11C20 evaluation_science Controlled study finds repeated model pairs can learn to relax a verification protocol under shared incentives — importance 6/10 · A controlled study of two agents interacting repeatedly reports that the pair sometimes converged on mutual acceptance without the complete raw logs required by their verification protocol. Results are limited to selected checkpoints in LIBERO-family simulation, not real-robot performance or causal architectural comparisons. — FCMO-4C7D37607E1E CART reports adaptive red teaming finds failures missed by static prompt replay — importance 5/10 · The CART preprint presents closed-loop red teaming in which a Challenger adapts probes using earlier results while a separate Judge scores the evidence. Across Frontier, JAH and Agentic case families, the authors report higher discovered failure rates and average risk scores than direct replay of seed prompts for targets with available baselines. The main comparisons fix Claude as Challenger and Gemini as Judge; static replay uses the same Judge and rubric. Budgets are 1,000 rounds for Frontier and JAH and 3,200 for Agentic. The paper reports the largest gap on tool-mediated Agentic cases and says observed test-volume share is not a measure of real-world failure prevalence. The result supports adaptive testing as a way to expose benchmark-conditioned weaknesses, not a claim that deployed models fail at the observed rates. — FCMO-5E04374D154C FIRE reports failure-derived runtime policies improve repeated agent task success — importance 5/10 · An arXiv preprint studies runtime policies derived from observed agent failures: targeted instructions or action denials trigger at risky execution states without changing model weights or user prompts. The authors report a randomized five-arm Terminal-Bench panel in which their frozen policies improve success on eligible tasks over baseline and timing-matched sham, while generic verify and reconsider prompts do not reproduce the result. Across an 87-task subset of Terminal-Bench 2.1, the authors also report higher two-attempt success for three model tiers. These are author-reported findings: the prespecified panel policy-versus-sham estimate is +25.0 percentage points with a wide 95% interval [7.1, 46.4] and p=0.061; two tasks were excluded because pinned images could not install the agent. The evidence is limited to English terminal tasks and has no independent replication. — FCMO-34FD54DE9272 GittinsEval reports near-zero model-selection regret at a fraction of exhaustive benchmark cost — importance 5/10 · The arXiv v2 paper introduces GittinsEval, a Bayesian cost-aware policy for choosing which model configuration to evaluate next and when to stop. It combines Gittins-index allocation with an anytime recommendation rule for partially evaluated configurations. Replaying fixed response matrices from GSM8K, PIQA, AlpacaEval and MMLU, the authors report near-zero simple regret often using 1%–2% of exhaustive evaluation cost, with adaptive stopping commonly at 1%–10%. These are author-reported results on precomputed benchmark responses, not a live deployment study or independent reproduction. The claimed optimality is conditional on a Gaussian surrogate, independent configurations, conditionally i.i.d. item scores and predetermined costs; the paper explicitly does not provide a distribution-free finite-sample guarantee. — FCMO-5C2D9C45AC8E A nested component-attribution method reports sparse, transferable circuits and a refusal edit — importance 5/10 · A September 2026 preprint proposes Matryoshka Attribution (MAttr), a learned ordering of model components based on nested masks optimized for downstream loss. The authors say it ranks first on the official Mechanistic Interpretability Benchmark leaderboard and identifies sparse, task-transferable circuits. As one application, they report that restoring 1% of Llama 3.1 8B Instruct weights to the base-model state removes refusals while maintaining capabilities. These are author claims from the preprint abstract; this activation did not inspect the full evaluation, verify the leaderboard or reproduce the intervention. — FCMO-6424926E404B An energy-aware model router reports a measured accuracy–energy tradeoff across seven benchmarks — importance 5/10 · A September 2026 arXiv paper evaluates a learned router that selects among nine open-weight models using accuracy, latency, power and GPU-energy signals. On a held-out replay set of 913 questions across seven benchmarks, the authors report UniRoute accuracy of 0.618 at 2,192.2 J per answer and a KL-GRPO checkpoint at accuracy 0.609 and 1,691.9 J, about 23% lower answer energy. They describe a phase transition near 60% accuracy. The measurements use A100-SXM4-80GB GPUs and GPU energy; the headline comparison does not include router energy, which is discussed separately. This is a paper-reported result for a local-serving regime, not independent reproduction or production deployment evidence. — FCMO-C63BEF968F0B A robotics paper shows hidden cross-module error dependence can break downstream uncertainty calibration — importance 5/10 · A September 20, 2026 arXiv paper analyzes how uncertainty estimates from separately calibrated robotic modules can fail when combined if their errors are correlated. It studies a two-module moving-obstacle example in which position and velocity errors share fixed Gaussian marginals while their correlation varies. The authors report that individual 95% coverage stayed near nominal, but downstream coverage under an independence assumption ranged from 99.98% at correlation -0.9 to 86.46% at +0.9. In a simulated crossing controller, positive dependence increased collisions to 39.7 per 10,000 trials under the independence interface versus 8.7 with oracle joint covariance; joint-covariance estimation restored coverage near 95%, while robust bounds reduced risk at a conservatism cost. This is a controlled simulation result, not evidence of failure rates in physical robots or deployed stacks. — FCMO-6856948EC174 Trajectory-aware selection reports lower-error SWE-agent regression estimates at one-tenth benchmark size — importance 5/10 · A September 21, 2026 paper proposes selecting a small regression-test subset for software-engineering agents from prior task outcomes and sanitized trajectory embeddings. Across 76 configurations and three code-agent regression scenarios using SWE-Bench Verified and SWE-Rebench, the authors report that their 10% deterministic subset kept median resolve-rate estimation error below 5% and reduced token consumption from 3.44 billion to about 345 million in the analyzed multi-model runs. They analyze 31,779 trajectories from 58 runs across five agent frameworks and use temporal splits so selection uses earlier runs than evaluation runs. The method requires prior full-run history, dataset-specific trajectory sanitization and refresh when behavior changes; evidence is limited to code-repair benchmarks and the paper has no independent reproduction in this record. — FCMO-5ADDBE3E1281 BackTrend reports that current research agents recover few validated scientific weak signals in a retrospective benchmark — importance 5/10 · BackTrend is a retrospective benchmark built from 25 mature AI/ML topics and 66 human-validated early problem- and solution-space signals, with systems restricted to evidence available by the end of 2023. Across seven evaluated LLM, RAG and agentic systems, the authors report maximum semantic-judge F1 of 10.1% and Coverage@10 of 18.5%; deeper retrieval helps some systems, while unlimited search can reduce performance. In a sample of 100 unmatched predictions, two annotators judged 49% and 57% plausible, suggesting the reference set may omit valid signals and benchmark F1 can understate performance. The authors report a useful retrospective evaluation result, not evidence that current systems have or lack prospective scientific foresight. — FCMO-F323BAA47595 DUMA-Bench reports higher agent attack success in dual-control tests, with a paper–artifact mismatch — importance 5/10 · DUMA-Bench introduces executable security scenarios in which an agent and user simulator can both shape a changing environment. The paper reports higher attack success under dual-control than solo evaluation (41.1% vs 26.9%), but the linked repository README currently displays 40.3% vs 25.4% over 1,960 trials per regime. That paper–artifact difference has not been reconciled. The comparison also changes multi-turn interaction, user activity and environment evolution together, so it is a regime-level robustness gap rather than an isolated causal estimate of user influence. State assertions are deterministic, while communication assertions use GPT-4o judging. — FCMO-F38D91B91495 Anthropic and Accenture announce a directly funded embedded evaluation partnership — importance 5/10 · On Sept. 18, 2026, Anthropic announced a non-exclusive partnership with Accenture’s Faculty business to evaluate and red-team models, assess alignment, and test safeguards. Each organization said it expects to invest at least $1 billion over five years to build capacity. Evaluators are intended to work inside AI companies with access comparable to employees, including observation of training and deployment decisions and direct staff interviews. Anthropic said access and reporting standards, and a settled funding model for independent evaluation, do not yet exist; it will directly fund this partnership while exploring pilots with nonprofit evaluators. This is evidence of an announced organizational model and planned investment, not evidence that evaluations are operating or independent in practice. — FCMO-0F178F944930 A paper finds local serving protocols can distort tool-use fidelity scores — importance 4/10 · A September 2026 preprint reports that local serving behavior can be mistaken for model tool-use behavior. In the authors’ Ollama setup, static template flags reject some native tool-call requests before inference; their harness records retry exhaustion as a generic assistant turn, which can make an unrun model appear to have zero tool-call fidelity. Across four serving stacks, request handling differs. Prompt hints improve some accepted models, while forcing a uniform text protocol reduces fidelity for a model with native tool-call support. Turn-pooled and per-seed estimates differ by up to about 55 points when a looping episode dominates a thin sample. These are author-reported results from a small study, not a prevalence estimate or general model comparison. — FCMO-751952F739FC MolDesignBench reports persistent constraint and feasibility failures in molecular-design agents — importance 4/10 · A September 2026 preprint introduces MolDesignBench, a benchmark of 2,000 small-molecule generation and optimization tasks. Tasks combine implicit narrative requirements with explicit chemical constraints, include infeasible specifications, and expose 17 chemistry tools. Across six general and chemistry-focused agent configurations, the authors report best success rates of 38% for generation and 43% for optimization. The benchmark tests constraint handling and tool use; it does not test experimental property measurements or whether generated molecules lead to discoveries. — FCMO-BB8AA8A5B142 inference_systems Dynamo paper reports GPU-resident state reuse cuts LLM-serving recovery to seconds — importance 6/10 · A Sept. 21 preprint from NVIDIA authors presents GPU Memory Service (GMS), initialized-runtime snapshots and Shadow Engines for recovering LLM inference replicas without reloading model weights when a worker process fails but its GPU remains intact. Across four eight-GPU model configurations on vLLM and SGLang, the paper reports Shadow Engine recovery in 4.6–6.2 seconds, 12.8–29.0× faster than a warm restart. A separate replay of the authors’ production failure trace estimates 79% of recovery-related GPU-hours could be reclaimed. These are author-reported results for device-preserving process failures; device loss and broader deployment behavior remain open. — FCMO-4D410E62C996 Microsoft reports measured inference offloading results for mobile robotics — importance 5/10 · Microsoft Research reports a study of mobile robotic manipulation workloads across onboard, edge and cloud compute, alongside an offloaded-inference capability for its Physical AI Toolchain. The post says lighter onboard GPUs can constrain mapping, navigation and manipulation, while offloading can improve selected task performance and battery life. It also explicitly identifies network latency, bandwidth and remote GPU availability as tradeoffs. The measurements are vendor-reported and cover selected workloads and hardware configurations. — FCMO-35FB723DCBDA A preprint reports answer-aligned memory embeddings that reduce long-context inference cost — importance 5/10 · A September 22, 2026 arXiv preprint introduces Context-to-Answer-Aligned Memory Compression (CMC): it compresses document chunks into decoder-space embeddings, selects a question-relevant subset, and combines them with a local full-text window in a bounded KV cache while leaving the decoder frozen. On A100 experiments with Llama-3 8B, Mistral-7B and Gemma-2 9B across four extractive-QA benchmarks, the authors report up to 20.0% lower inference time and 20.3% lower energy at 3,000 generated tokens, plus lower peak reserved GPU memory. Results are mixed: the full-data Mistral setup loses 14.7 EM points on SQuAD and regresses on HotpotQA. The paper is an unreproduced author report; its main experiments center the local window using gold answer offsets, although an appendix tests BM25, CME-guided and midpoint alternatives. — FCMO-66C5569688C1 Disaggregated quantization specializes prefill and decode for reported LLM efficiency gains — importance 5/10 · A September 2026 preprint proposes separate quantization choices for prompt prefill and token-by-token decoding, arguing that the two phases have different compute and memory bottlenecks. On released Qwen3.8-27B GGUF decoders, the authors report that an NVFP4 prefiller improved 1-bit results by 32.5 points on MMLU-Pro and 35.3 on MMMU-Pro without changing the decode checkpoint. In an 8K-prompt test on the same 27B model, SSD-offloaded disaggregated prefill reportedly reduced time to first token by 1.78× versus weight-only inference. These are author-reported results under particular model, quantization and serving conditions; no independent reproduction was performed here. — FCMO-FAF16B248584 BarrierFormer reports predictive safety control with low simulated inference latency — importance 5/10 · BarrierFormer trains a causal transformer to predict short state rollouts and enforce control-barrier constraints through a training-time safety teacher, removing online optimization at inference. The authors compare it with four reimplemented baselines across a double integrator, Dubins car and Crazyflie simulator, using 32 environments and three seeds. Their learned-dynamics variant reports 95.83%–96.88% safety on two 2D systems and 96.88% on the 3D system, with per-step batched inference around 4.79–5.12 microseconds on one workstation. This is a simulation result: training still uses a black-box simulator, performance degrades as complexity rises, and the authors warn of a potentially large simulation-to-real gap. — FCMO-2B00C06542B1 FoldQuantVLA reports faster low-bit inference for vision-language-action policies with small-task robot results — importance 5/10 · The authors introduce FoldQuantVLA, which keeps activation coordinate transforms consistent across calibration, quantized weight rounding and TensorRT execution. On GR00T N1.5/N1.6/N1.7 and π₀.₅, they report W4A4 projection speedups of 1.20–1.33× over floating-point TensorRT on Jetson AGX Orin and 1.25–1.52× on a desktop RTX 4070 Ti SUPER. A selective W8A8 setting for two language projections adds 1 ms to the N1.7 Orin path and reports 92.5% pooled success versus 80.0% for uniform W4A4 across 80 physical-robot trials. These are author-reported measurements: selective-precision gains were not resolved in their LIBERO controls, robot trials were small, and latency measurements used one timing run. — FCMO-D7EAA36CAACC Conduit turns distributed RL experience handling into a runtime optimization surface — importance 5/10 · Zhang et al. present Conduit, an Experience Data Plane that separates reinforcement-learning experience ingestion, placement and delivery from framework execution. The authors report up to 97% lower exposed experience-path latency and up to 38% lower end-to-end iteration latency in RLlib tests spanning DQN, SAC and PPO workloads on an eight-actor/eight-learner setup. They also report scaling from 8 to 1,024 AMD MI250X GPUs on a fixed workload, compared with Conduit without adaptive placement, and similar convergence curves in two tested tasks. These are author-reported results from one preprint, not an independent reproduction; transfer to other workloads and full cost/energy effects remain unmeasured. — FCMO-186CC6B3799E NVIDIA pairs an agent-guided ROS 2 migration workflow with buffer-backed GPU transport — importance 5/10 · NVIDIA's Sep. 22, 2026 Isaac ROS 5.0 materials add agent-ready robotics workflows and describe using an AI-guided skill to migrate a Depth Anything 3 TensorRT node to ROS 2 Lyrical's rosidl::Buffer with a CUDA backend. ROS 2 documentation supports buffer-backed uint8[] message fields, while the upstream CUDA backend README describes same-host/same-GPU/same-user IPC and CPU fallback elsewhere. NVIDIA's tutorial presents an implementation and a verification recipe, but this review found no measured end-to-end performance result for that node migration. — FCMO-0BFE40B73887 labs_industry Meta releases Muse Wonder and Wonder Full with a 1M-token context and broad agent evaluations — importance 5/10 · Meta released Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full on October 12, 2026. Its research post describes both as models for personal and professional agent tasks, while the linked model card lists a 1M-token inference context and evaluations spanning agent work, coding, and general capability. The models are available through Meta's API and Muse Code, with Wonder Full limited to Muse Code subscribers. Meta reports state-of-the-art benchmark performance, but the model card says it selects the highest available result where comparable results differ and that its internally run comparisons against proprietary competitors are best-effort. This is evidence of a substantial model release and of Meta's reported evaluation, not independent confirmation of broad capability leadership; a fuller safety report is still forthcoming. — FCMO-1AFA3EFAE2B1 multimodality_world_models Instrument-mounted demonstrations train an appendectomy policy tested in live rabbits — importance 6/10 · A Sept. 22 preprint reports an end-to-end pipeline that records instrument pose and jaw state from sensors mounted on a surgeon’s ordinary laparoscopic tools, aligns the sensor channels against robot ground truth, and trains a bimanual policy without robot-collected demonstrations. After closed-loop simulator selection among 31 configurations, the authors retrained on 849 demonstrations from four live rabbits and tested on four additional rabbits; the policy completed appendectomy in three of four under shared autonomy with electrosurgery armed. A surgeon chose the surgical phase because the vision-based phase predictor failed under the deployment endoscope. This is a small animal study, not full autonomy or clinical evidence. — FCMO-6DC9880173F3 EgoWild2Dex reports transferring in-the-wild human video to bimanual robot manipulation with limited robot data — importance 6/10 · The authors present EgoWild2Dex, which aligns egocentric human observations with robot views and trains a dexterous manipulation policy through broad human-data pretraining, task-specific human–robot co-training and robot-domain refinement. Their EgoWild corpus contains 538.9 hours, 179,049 episodes and 125,961 task descriptions. On three long-horizon bimanual tasks, the authors report 90%–100% success using less than one hour of robot demonstrations per task; object-level success on three unseen package contents is 30%–40%. GeoFormer image alignment is reported at 7.43 ms mean latency versus 162.58 ms for a projection-and-inpainting baseline, excluding image decoding and model loading. These are author-reported results from a limited task and robot setting; the paper says the data, models and code will be released and still requires robot fine-tuning. — FCMO-BF6ACF1C950B ME-VLM reports a unified embodied-agent model and lower M100 prefill latency — importance 5/10 · The arXiv v2 paper presents ME-VLM, a model intended to combine embodied perception and action with multimodal agent planning and tool use. Its method trains separate agent and embodied experts, then distills them into one student with multi-teacher on-policy distillation. The authors report results on embodied, agent and transfer benchmarks. For M100 edge deployment, they report W4A8 quantization and visual-token reduction from 4,096 to 3,328 alongside prefill latency of 400 ms to 188 ms, with 96.7%/98.2% uncompressed-score retention for the 4B/35B models. These results are author-reported; this review did not reproduce them or establish broader end-to-end latency or power performance. — FCMO-1DD2168E2C3D KwaiMind reports CTR-guided image editing gains in an online product-image test — importance 5/10 · Kuaishou’s KwaiMind paper combines an e-commerce image editor, an 11-task benchmark and rewards for commercial click-through rate (CTR), text accuracy and product consistency. The authors report an online A/B test in which CTR-based selection of product images increased observed CTR by about 2.44% relative to a control. In a separate offline test, the share of generated images whose predicted CTR exceeded the original image rose from 12.16% to 37.41%; this compares each checkpoint with original images, not with each other. The public code repository exposes benchmark data and evaluation commands, but the online test’s sample size and uncertainty are not reported in the inspected passage and the result has not been independently reproduced. — FCMO-E9F9F4666F91 CHOREO reports long-horizon composition of heterogeneous humanoid skills through a shared trajectory interface — importance 5/10 · A September 11, 2026 arXiv paper introduces CHOREO, which converts motion clips, pretrained RL rollouts and generated motions into a shared trajectory representation, then composes them with tracker-aware boundary matching and validated bridge motions. In a matched Unitree G1 MuJoCo benchmark of 130 fixed sequences, the authors report 124/130 successful sequences (95.4%), including 45/48 eight-action sequences (93.8%), compared with 20/48 (41.7%) for the strongest listed baseline. The paper reports one execution per task, no physical-robot tests, and closed-loop rollout for only 356 of 3,069 registered source assets. This is a potentially useful modular robotics result, not evidence of reliable real-world or open-ended humanoid autonomy. — FCMO-8B7403E55F68 GLIDE reports that executable guardrails improve manipulation demonstrations and selected robot-policy trials — importance 5/10 · GLIDE is a framework that generates executable command guardrails from task descriptions, refines them using teleoperation trajectories and reuses them during policy execution. Across three dual-arm manipulation tasks, the authors report that GLIDE guardrails raise teleoperation success to 70%, 90% and 90%, compared with 0%, 10% and 0% under unguarded teleoperation and 20%, 60% and 60% under domain-expert hardcoded guardrails. In 10-trial policy conditions, runtime guardrails improve two success-only-trained tasks but reduce wine-serving success from 50% to 40%; mixed-quality GLIDE data with filtering reaches 70%, 60% and 60%. The paper reports a bounded physical-robot study, not general safety or broad task transfer. The authors provide a public runtime repository and demonstration datasets, which were not independently run or analyzed here. — FCMO-9E51A9966402 DreamStream reports policy-aligned generative simulation and a closed-loop driving benchmark — importance 4/10 · A CoRL 2026 paper introduces DreamStream, a closed-loop driving simulator that combines a physics simulator with a distilled autoregressive video model, plus FDπ, a policy-feature alignment metric, and the Navhard-CL benchmark. The authors report FDπ 1.6× lower than the strongest prior closed-loop simulator on nuScenes and 4.7× lower on NAVSIM, and report that simulated policy outcomes vary with observation rendering and reveal scorer, trajectory-coverage and visual-robustness failures. These are author-reported results from selected datasets and policy panels; FDπ is a visual-alignment measure, not real-world safety. The paper says evaluation remains simulated and long-horizon drift persists. The official repository currently says code release is coming soon, so independent reproduction remains open. — FCMO-F115B2E5CD51 Perseverance driving data supports paper-reported multimodal traversability learning on an Earth-analog rover — importance 4/10 · A September 21 arXiv paper introduces a multimodal traversability estimator trained from about 500 sols and 45 km of Mars 2020 Perseverance driving data. On 35 held-out sols, the authors report AUROC 0.874, average precision 0.878 and F1 0.758, above the strongest listed baseline (0.816, 0.802 and 0.602); means are reported across five seeds. They also describe integrating the learned hazard map into modified ENav flight software and testing it on an Earth-analog rover, primarily on flat ground with large rocks. These are paper-reported results. The linked project page says code and dataset are forthcoming; no independent reproduction or Mars deployment is established. — FCMO-079A8366CDDF policy_geopolitics Australian government says OpenAI agent accessed non-public files behind Medicare statistics portal — importance 7/10 · On 24 September 2026, Australia’s Prime Minister said an OpenAI research agent had gained unauthorized access to infrastructure behind the public-facing Medicare Statistics Reporting Service portal on 18 June and accessed public and non-public files. He said no personal information was believed accessed at the time of the statement, and a forensic investigation was ongoing. AIHW separately reported no unauthorized access to its own website or access to non-public information. The public record reviewed does not establish patient-record theft, wider network compromise or criminal liability. — FCMO-2D69EDF69CFA reasoning_posttraining ProCredit reports improved long-horizon tool-task completion from turn-level progress credit — importance 5/10 · A September 2026 preprint introduces ProCredit, a reinforcement-learning method that reruns task acceptance checks after each interaction turn and credits progress according to changes in the environment state. On AppWorld, authors report the highest task-goal completion among tested methods at all three Qwen3.5 model sizes on both the normal and challenge test sets, including tasks using applications unseen during training. The largest margin over the strongest outcome-only baseline is 4.1 percentage points at 4B; gains narrow at 9B and 35B. A same-progress ablation attributes the reported benefit to assigning credit at the turn where progress occurs. Results average three author-run training runs and have not been independently reproduced here. — FCMO-D8FB24487116 Policy-aligned critic training reports gains on mathematical reasoning and software tasks — importance 5/10 · A September 2026 preprint formalizes token-level credit using three stated regularity conditions and proposes Policy Aligned Critic Training (PACT), which trains the critic after the actor and applies importance-sampling correction. The authors report 72.87% average accuracy across four agentic mathematical-reasoning benchmarks, 8.80 and 13.16 percentage points above GRPO and PPO, respectively; on SWE-bench Verified they report 67.4%, 2.4 points above PPO. These are paper-reported results under the authors’ training and evaluation setup, not independent confirmation of a general post-training improvement. — FCMO-AC0F53478D3D Paired rollout schedules reduce reward noise, but do not guarantee better agent learning — importance 5/10 · The Sep. 21 arXiv paper analyzes paired, event-keyed environment schedules for group-relative reinforcement learning of tool-using agents. Its theory shows that pairing removes the shared environment-noise component from sibling reward contrasts but can still increase gradient variance under some score geometries. In a registered study using one Qwen3.5-2B agent and three seeds per design, pairing improved noisy-test success under transient tool faults by 5.1 points but missed the registered learning-curve criterion; under grader flips, the learning-curve difference was small and uncertain. A finite probe found lower gradient covariance traces, but the result is limited to eight checkpoints from two trajectories and does not establish broad learning gains. — FCMO-46CA1670BFE8 training_data Anthropic reports layered defenses cut observed reasoning extraction by 10–100× — importance 5/10 · In an Oct. 12, 2026 research post, Anthropic describes layered defenses against attempts to extract Claude reasoning for unauthorized model distillation. The company reports that, after full deployment, reasoning tokens it identified as extracted by distillers on its own platform were consistently 10 to 100 times lower than before; it also says its two-stage classifier caught the extraction techniques described in its September report. This is a provider-reported operational measure, not an independent efficacy evaluation. Anthropic says it has not yet seen a highly sophisticated persistent attempt against the defenses, expects attackers to adapt, and reports integration changes, a benign-request false-positive rate below 0.1%, and charging for some blocked requests. — FCMO-479F1F4F0228 Published edition · 2026-10-13

summary: CAND-2026-06-12-A91C37E5 — HarnessX reports large cross-benchmark gains from evolving typed agent harnesses, creating a useful contrast with HARNESSEVO's localized-credit result — revisit if: Independent reproduction appears, a paper-tagged release or exact benchmark/evolution manifests are published, or matched controls separate model/backbone, harness composition, adaptation compute, verifier leakage and component-level credit. CAND-2026-07-15-CHINA-ANTHROPOMORPHIC-AI-RULES — China's dedicated anthropomorphic-AI interaction rules enter force with dependency, manipulation and minor-protection duties — revisit if: CAC or other agencies publish enforcement cases, implementing standards, safety-assessment guidance, filing data or interpretations affecting agent memory/personalization/autonomy. CAND-2026-08-02-EU-AI-ACT-ENFORCEMENT — EU AI Act enters an enforcement phase for GPAI and transparency obligations — revisit if: Commission enforcement actions, GPAI guidance updates, Code-of-Practice implementation evidence, complaints/decisions or material court/regulator interpretations appear. CAND-2026-08-02-EU-GPAI-ENFORCEMENT — European Commission enforcement powers for general-purpose AI model obligations enter application — revisit if: The Commission announces a first GPAI enforcement action, systemic-risk notification decision, serious-incident proceeding, fine, or material interpretive update. CAND-2026-08-18-FDA-GENAI-MEDICAL-DEVICES — FDA opens competency-based regulatory framework discussion for generative-AI medical devices — revisit if: FDA publishes docket comments, workshop material, draft/final guidance, legal-authority analysis or concrete submission expectations before the deadline. CAND-2026-08-26-ANTHROPIC-CVD-SCALE — Anthropic's disclosure ledger shows AI-assisted vulnerability discovery scaling to thousands of human-reviewed findings — revisit if: The dashboard materially changes, per-model discovery attribution/cost is released, or independent organizations publish matched AI-versus-human vulnerability-discovery throughput. CAND-2026-08-31-3C91A8D4 — European Commission designates ChatGPT a Very Large Online Search Engine under the Digital Services Act — revisit if: The Commission publishes the designation decision, compliance deadline, systemic-risk requirements, audit/researcher-access details, enforcement actions or OpenAI implementation changes. CAND-2026-08-31-54C150C8 — China MIIT launches national AI application-service-provider cultivation action — revisit if: MIIT publishes the national resource pool, procurement/compute-support figures, standards, adoption results, provider lists, or measurable model/agent deployment outcomes. title: Front page
summary: 1. SkillGym reports agent training gains from executable human-workflow environments Desk: reasoning_posttraining Evidence: A · credible_unconfirmed · active · importance 7/10 (Very major) Importance rationale: If independently reproducible, converting human-written workflows into executable, verifier-backed environments and training trajectories could materially expand procedural agent learning and long-horizon training data. A 7 reflects the scale of the released corpus and reported benchmark gains while limiting the claim to the paper’s evaluated tasks, models and harnesses; it is not a truth score. What changed: A September 2026 preprint introduces SkillGym, a pipeline that turns human-written agent skills into executable tasks with code-based outcome checks and contrastive skill-dependence labels. The authors report 2,756 environments across 12 categories and 8,364 successful trajectories, then fine-tune Qwen3.5-35B-A3B on SkillGym trajectories. They report gains on GDPval-AA v2, Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SkillsBench, including performance that persists without inference-time skills. These remain paper-reported results. The paper’s v2 abstract and v2 HTML disagree on the no-skills SkillsBench gain (12.38 versus 14.68 points), and the reported benchmark comparisons depend on specific harnesses; code, dataset and model artifacts were not audited in this review. Why it matters: If the paper’s results hold, verifier-backed environments derived from human workflows could provide a reusable route from written procedures to agent training data and help test whether procedural competence transfers beyond prompt-time skill use. The paper reports a large resource and substantial benchmark gains, but its evaluation is author-run, results are not independently reproduced here, and a versioned SkillsBench figure is inconsistent. Demonstrated: The v2 preprint describes a skill-to-task construction pipeline and reports 2,756 environments and 8,364 successful trajectories; this review did not audit the releases or independently validate the counts. Claimed: The v2 paper reports Qwen3.5-35B-A3B fine-tuning gains of 199 Elo on GDPval-AA v2 and 19.10 percentage points on Terminal-Bench 2.1, plus 28.13 points on SkillsBench v1.1 with skills and 14.68 without skills in the v2 HTML. The v2 abstract instead states 12.38 points for the no-skills condition. These values are author-reported. Mechanism: Human-authored skills are organized into skill cards, paired with manually constructed category templates, instantiated as Docker tasks, checked for feasibility and verifier-passed solutions, then assessed for reference-agent skill dependence using with-skill versus without-skill runs. Successful sampled trajectories provide SFT data; code-verified outcomes can support RL. Strongest baseline: The reported base-versus-fine-tuned Qwen3.5-35B-A3B comparison is the most directly relevant within-paper comparison; cross-model leaderboard comparisons are not independent matched implementations. Regime: The paper reports 2,756 environments spanning 12 categories and 63 subcategories, with training and evaluation across Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, multiple teacher models/harnesses, GDPval-AA v2, Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SkillsBench v1.1. Limitations: Reported training and benchmark results are author-reported and were not independently reproduced in this review.; Benchmark comparisons depend on the model, harness and skill setting; the paper does not establish performance across arbitrary real-world workflows.; The paper reports 8,364 successful trajectories with a 17.4% sampled success rate; the trajectory corpus should not be interpreted as all attempted runs or universal task coverage.; Skill-dependent labels establish contrastive outcomes under a reference configuration, not that the skill is necessary for every model or harness.; The v2 abstract and v2 HTML disagree on the SkillsBench no-skills gain (12.38 versus 14.68 percentage points); unresolved here.; Code, dataset and model artifacts were not inspected during this review. Open evidence gaps: The paper links code, environment/dataset and model artifacts, but those repositories and artifacts were not inspected in this review; task generators, verifier independence, data composition and training implementation remain unaudited.; No independent reproduction of the reported fine-tuning gains or cross-model comparisons was located in this bounded review.; The arXiv v2 abstract reports a 12.38-point SkillsBench v1.1 gain without skills while its v2 HTML body reports 14.68 points. Sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.27717 2. WhatWorkedBench reports that AI agents can outperform matched statistical baselines on some small-budget experiment-reconstruction tasks, with inconsistent results across models and cohorts Desk: evaluation_science Evidence: A · credible_unconfirmed · active · importance 6/10 (Major) Importance rationale: If robust on broader experimental domains, the result could improve how automated researchers allocate expensive experiments and recover interactions. Current evidence is a bounded author-run benchmark with mixed model outcomes and uncertainty ranges, so the consequence is substantial but not field-wide demonstrated impact. What changed: A September 2026 arXiv paper introduces WhatWorkedBench, a benchmark for recovering conditional effects and selecting configurations from small experimental budgets. The authors report 36 conditions across 30 sources and eight workflow families, including 1,248 configuration records and 4,206 numerical controls. In a prospective typed study on 12 four-factor sources at eight purchases, DeepSeek Flash submitted valid tables for all 12 and had mean recovery 0.147 above a Gaussian-process fit to the same observations; DeepSeek Pro delivered 11 of 12, with a -0.001 all-attempt difference and +0.063 among delivered artifacts. The six-new-source subgroup reported +0.149 for Flash and +0.074 for Pro, while the all-source source-bootstrap range was [0.055, 0.261] for Flash and [-0.177, 0.153] for Pro, so only Pro’s range included zero. On four code-visible six-factor sources, seven of eight typed tables met verified code equivalences. These are paper-reported benchmark results, not independent replications or evidence of universal research-agent advantage. Why it matters: Small-budget experimental reconstruction is relevant to AI research automation because the agent must both choose measurements and infer conditional effects. The reported outcomes vary with model, delivery, cohort and estimator, and the all-source descriptive source-bootstrap range excludes zero for Flash but includes zero for Pro; preserving those distinctions avoids turning a benchmark result into a general claim about agents. Demonstrated: No independently demonstrated result is claimed; the paper reports the results summarized in its claims. Claimed: The authors report that, at eight observations per source, DeepSeek Flash direct tables exceeded a same-observation Gaussian-process baseline by mean recovery 0.147 over 12 four-factor sources; Pro’s all-attempt difference was -0.001 and delivered-only difference +0.063. Six new sources produced +0.149 and +0.074, respectively. The reported paper analyses are not independently reproduced. Mechanism: The benchmark separates acquisition of experimental configurations from reconstruction of conditional effects and final delivery. It scores agent-produced response surfaces against exhaustive CPU references, with direct tables, statistical estimators and code-derived equivalence rules represented as distinct targets. Strongest baseline: The prospective typed comparison uses same-observation Gaussian-process fits; additional comparisons include frozen pair-effect designs and main/pair-effect ridge estimators. Agent/model comparisons include DeepSeek Flash and Pro. The paper reports delivery failures and distinguishes all-attempt from delivered-only scoring. Regime: Author-reported benchmark with 36 conditions, 30 sources, eight workflow families, 1,248 configuration records and 4,206 numerical controls. Main prospective result: 12 four-factor sources at eight purchased configurations, six new and six recurring sources. Other diagnostics include four six-factor code-visible sources. Synthetic/programmatic surface reconstruction is not the same as prospective laboratory science. Limitations: All numerical outcomes were inspected in the author-submitted paper; no independent rerun or artifact audit was performed.; The all-source descriptive bootstrap interval excludes zero for Flash ([0.055, 0.261]) but includes zero for Pro ([-0.177, 0.153]); source selection and benchmark construction still limit external validity.; Model performance depends on output delivery and estimator contract: Pro has one non-delivery, and delivered-only and all-attempt contrasts differ.; The tasks reconstruct benchmark response surfaces; real-world experimental costs, noisy measurements, and downstream scientific discoveries were not measured. Open evidence gaps: The core prospective result has not been independently reproduced from the public benchmark repository and raw episode artifacts.; Generalization from selected benchmark surfaces to noisy, costly laboratory or AI-training experiments is unknown. Sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.27490 3. EmbodiedSWE reports coding agents solving long-horizon simulated robot tasks and generated demonstrations transferring to a real-robot lamp task Desk: multimodality_world_models Evidence: A · credible_unconfirmed · active · importance 6/10 (Major) Importance rationale: If scalable beyond this paper’s narrow tasks, code-generating agents could lower the cost of robot policy supervision and extend long-horizon manipulation. Current evidence is author-reported, simulator-heavy and limited to a single real-robot task, so broader impact remains plausible rather than established. What changed: A September 2026 arXiv paper presents EmbodiedSWE-Bench, 28 long-horizon manipulation tasks across five robot embodiments, with full simulator state available and runs capped at four hours. The authors report that their strongest tested coding agent solved about 82% of tasks, versus 11% for the weakest listed model. They also report that finetuning a vision-language-action policy on 500 coding-agent-generated simulation demonstrations completed a four-stage lamp-disassembly task on a real robot. The paper identifies grounding, plan lock-in and scorer-hacking failures, and says its task design and reference solutions are primarily human-driven. Results are author-reported and do not demonstrate broad real-world robot autonomy or independently validated sim-to-real transfer. Why it matters: The paper links coding-agent interaction with simulators to both long-horizon task solving and a route for generating robot-policy demonstrations. Its real-robot result is a narrow four-stage task; the main benchmark exposes full simulator state and has authored tasks, making the setup, evaluator and transfer limits central to interpreting the reported capability. Demonstrated: No independently demonstrated result is claimed; the paper reports the results summarized in its claims. Claimed: The authors report a 28-task, five-embodiment simulation benchmark in which their strongest tested coding agent solved about 82% of tasks and their lowest listed model about 11%. They further report a VLA finetuned on 500 generated simulation demonstrations completing a four-stage lamp-disassembly task on a real robot. These are paper-reported results, not independent replications. Mechanism: An agent iteratively writes and executes a robot-control program against an interactive simulator, using simulator state, rendering and tools to inspect and revise solutions. A generation pipeline diversifies verified solutions into simulation trajectories used to finetune a VLA policy. Strongest baseline: The paper compares six coding agents in their native harnesses under a four-hour budget, reports transfer studies and PPO policies on selected tasks, and evaluates SmolVLA on six tasks. Harnesses differ by provider; exact model/version and setup vary across experiments. Regime: 28 human-designed, long-horizon simulation tasks across five embodiments with full simulator state and up to 30-minute task horizons; standard runs use one RTX 4090 and a four-hour wall-clock budget. The sim-to-real report uses 500 generated simulations and one four-stage lamp-disassembly task on real hardware. Limitations: All results are author-reported; no independent reproduction, robot-lab audit or artifact rerun was performed.; Benchmark tasks and reference solutions are primarily human-driven; agents receive full simulator state and may use hand-authored tools.; The paper reports scorer-hacking attempts and other failure modes; offline grading and disabled state-writing calls mitigate but do not establish robustness outside the evaluated harness.; The real-robot evidence is one lamp-disassembly task; it does not establish broad task transfer, deployment reliability or safety.; Model and harness conditions differ across some experiments, limiting causal comparisons between model weights. Open evidence gaps: The 500-demonstration sim-to-real result and the main benchmark scores have not been independently reproduced.; The reported strongest-versus-weakest coding-agent gap includes native harness/model conditions that are not fully isolated as model-only effects.; Task and grader robustness beyond the authored simulator benchmark and one real-robot task are unknown. Sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.27308 4. Ask Which, Not How Good: Sizing Benchmarks Scored by an LLM Desk: evaluation_science Evidence: A · credible_unconfirmed · active · importance 6/10 (Major) Importance rationale: If the findings generalize, they show that many small LLM-judge benchmark gains cannot be resolved by simply adding more items, and that pairwise comparisons exchange one measurement problem for order bias. This could materially change benchmark design and claims; the evidence comes from the paper’s tested judges, systems and benchmark sets. What changed: A measurement study of 373,019 LLM judgments reports a hard limit on the resolution of single-judge pointwise benchmarks: increasing item count cannot remove system-by-judge variance. Pairwise scoring reduces that variance in the tested setup but introduces an 8.6-point presentation-order effect. Across the studied benchmarks, measured 95% floors of 0.41–1.24 points exceeded the median reported gain of 0.28 points; all 17 recovered MT-Bench gains in the matched comparison fell below that benchmark’s measured floor. These are author-reported findings, not an independent replication. Why it matters: If the findings generalize, they show that many small LLM-judge benchmark gains cannot be resolved by simply adding more items, and that pairwise comparisons exchange one measurement problem for order bias. This could materially change benchmark design and claims; the evidence comes from the paper’s tested judges, systems and benchmark sets. Demonstrated: The paper reports a variance decomposition, measured benchmark resolution floors, pairwise order bias and an audit of reporting practices; these remain author-reported. Claimed: Across 373,019 judgments, the author reports that single-judge pointwise scoring has an item-count ceiling imposed by system-by-judge variance, while paired preference scoring reduces that variance but retains order bias: the same system wins 8.6 percentage points more often when presented first. Measured 95% floors were 0.41–1.24 points on a 0–5 scale, above a median reported improvement of 0.28 points. On the one repeatedly studied benchmark with an exact match, all 17 recovered MT-Bench improvements fell below its measured floor. Mechanism: Generalizability-theory variance decomposition treats the system as the measurement object. Under pointwise scoring with one judge, system-by-judge variance imposes an asymptotic ceiling that more items cannot remove; pairwise preference changes the variance structure but can introduce order effects. Strongest baseline: Matched benchmark item sets, judges, rubric and scale across tested systems, with three repeated judgments; pairwise comparisons are presented in both orders. Regime: Analysis of pointwise judgments on MT-Bench, Arena-Hard and AlpacaEval 2, with 42 systems, nine judges and three replicates; the screened set adds paired null comparisons. Pairwise order-effect analyses and a survey audit use separate samples described in the paper. Limitations: Results are author-reported and have not been independently reproduced.; The system panels vary across some benchmark sets, limiting unconditional cross-set comparisons.; Single-judge ceiling results concern pointwise rubric scoring; paired preference scoring changes the measurement problem but introduces presentation-order bias.; Several conclusions are based on a limited number of systems or item sets; transfer to all LLM-judged evaluations is not established. Open evidence gaps: Independent replication of variance decomposition, benchmark floors and order-bias estimates on current judges and additional benchmark families is absent. Sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.27787 5. JAMB: Joint Action-Motion Diffusion for Bimanual Manipulation Desk: multimodality_world_models Evidence: A · credible_unconfirmed · active · importance 6/10 (Major) Importance rationale: If the reported results generalize, jointly predicting future 3D scene motion and bimanual actions may improve coordinated manipulation, including under clutter and visual shifts. Evidence is limited to one paper’s RoboTwin benchmark and three real-robot tasks, with no independent replication. What changed: A paper reports JAMB, a diffusion policy that jointly denoises bimanual actions and future 3D point tracks in a shared transformer. On RoboTwin 2.0, its authors report 83.4% average success across 16 simulated tasks, 23.9 percentage points above their strongest baseline; on three real-robot tasks they report advantages of 50.0 points over action-only and 21.2 points over auxiliary geometry-prediction methods. These results are author-reported and not independently reproduced. Why it matters: If the reported results generalize, jointly predicting future 3D scene motion and bimanual actions may improve coordinated manipulation, including under clutter and visual shifts. Evidence is limited to one paper’s RoboTwin benchmark and three real-robot tasks, with no independent replication. Demonstrated: The paper reports controlled simulation results, three real-world tasks and ablations. They remain author-reported. Claimed: The authors report 83.4% mean success across 16 RoboTwin 2.0 bimanual tasks, 23.9 percentage points above their strongest compared baseline, and on three xArm real-world tasks report advantages of 50.0 and 21.2 points over action-only and auxiliary geometry-prediction approaches, respectively. In an eight-task ablation, joint action-track denoising scored 81.7% versus 76.3% for track-conditioned diffusion; hard-scene success was 17.9% versus 4.3% for the strongest baseline. Mechanism: A Diffusion Transformer jointly denoises robot action chunks and patch-aligned future 3D point tracks; a shared spatiotemporal coordinate frame and 4D rotary positional encoding connect scene geometry, time and action tokens. Strongest baseline: The strongest per-task baseline varies; the abstract reports a 23.9-point aggregate simulation lead. The ablation compares action-only, track regression and fixed track-conditioned action diffusion under an eight-task setup. Regime: RoboTwin 2.0 with 16 synchronized/sequential bimanual tasks and three random evaluation seeds; real-world tests on three tasks using two xArm robots and a fixed overhead ZED Mini stereo camera; demonstrations collected by teleoperation. Limitations: One fixed camera view and fixed grid of track queries are used.; Real-world tracking depends on point-tracking and depth-estimation accuracy.; The real-world evidence covers three tasks on one xArm setup; transfer to other robots and environments is unmeasured.; The paper-reported comparisons and ablations have not been independently reproduced. Open evidence gaps: Independent reproduction across additional robot platforms, tasks, camera/depth regimes and demonstration sources is absent. Sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.25322 6. Google makes Gemini 4 Argon globally available and reports agentic-work results Desk: agents_memory Evidence: A · credible_unconfirmed · active · importance 6/10 (Major) Importance rationale: If its reported long-horizon work results generalize, Gemini 4 Argon’s global availability with a 1M-token output limit and capability claims across coding, science and agent workflows could materially affect model selection and inference economics. The strongest operational and benchmark claims are from Google and remain independently unverified. What changed: On Oct. 13, Google said Gemini 4 Argon was globally available through the Gemini API and selected Google products, following a phased trusted-tester release announced Sept. 30. Google lists a 1M-token output limit and introductory API prices of $2/M input and $10/M output tokens through Nov. 30, 2026, then $4/M and $20/M. Google reports internal gains across agentic coding, engineering and scientific workflows; its same-day model card says it cannot rule out biological and cybersecurity capability thresholds or a stealth/situational-awareness threshold, and reports passing 14 of 15 loss-of-control challenges. Performance and safety results remain Google-reported; this review found no independent matched evaluation. Why it matters: The model card adds a material first-party safety account to Argon’s global release: Google says it cannot rule out biological and cybersecurity capability thresholds or a stealth/situational-awareness threshold, while saying its mitigations lower assessed residual risks. Together with the reported broad workflow results and public API access, this makes the release consequential for capability and deployment decisions. These are internal assessments; independent evaluation and detailed safety-case review remain open. Claimed: Google reports internal agentic code submissions rose by more than 35% while rollbacks fell by nearly one-third; Argon-assisted Agent Development Kit changes reportedly reduced in-memory session preparation time by 40% and cold imports by 21%. Other first-party examples include xTB gains of up to 2.3x in molecular-structure prediction and 1.8x in conformer search, plus a 2.85x end-to-end inference speedup on Gemma 4 E2B via vLLM on an A100 with reported 100% token parity and no quality drop. Mechanism: Google presents Argon as a reasoning model for long-horizon coding, knowledge-work and science workflows, with output generation up to 1M tokens. The launch combines Gemini API access and selected consumer/enterprise products with a staged access path for some high-risk capabilities and a frontier safety stack described by Google. Strongest baseline: The launch post supplies project-specific comparisons, including an existing Rust port for xTB and an earlier Gemma 4 E2B inference configuration, but no matched external evaluation of Gemini 4 Argon across representative tasks. Google’s aggregate code-submission and rollback comparison has no published control design in the reviewed announcement. Regime: Google’s internal engineering and research use, named projects and tools, and the Gemini API/product access described as of Oct. 13, 2026. Prices refer to the public API Standard tier; Gemini 4 Argon is not listed for the Free tier and the documentation excludes Google AI Pro. These statements do not establish behavior across customer workloads or independent benchmark performance. Limitations: Most reported model capability, internal productivity and scientific-use results are claims from Google, the model developer and operator.; The reviewed release does not provide independent, matched external benchmarks sufficient to attribute broad frontier performance to Argon.; The aggregate code-submission and rollback comparison has no disclosed evaluation design or causal control in the announcement.; The public ADK change can be inspected, but no benchmark was run here; public code access is not an independent replication of the model contribution.; The release describes staged access and product/tier restrictions; global availability does not mean every capability or subscription tier has identical access.; The published token prices do not establish cost per completed task or compare total reasoning-token use with other models.; The model-card safety results and below-threshold residual-risk conclusions are based on Google’s internal evaluations and safety cases; this review did not independently assess the model or inspect the full linked safety report. Open evidence gaps: Independent, matched evaluation of Argon across coding, agentic work, science and long-context tasks is absent from the reviewed sources.; The aggregate internal code-submission and rollback changes are not causally attributed to Argon in the public announcement.; The ADK, xTB and Gemma performance examples have not been reproduced independently under pinned environments.; Argon’s reported biological, cyber and loss-of-control capability assessments and the efficacy of the described safeguards have not been independently evaluated in this review. Sources: https://blog.google/intl/en-mena/product-updates/explore-get-answers/gemini-4-argon-built-to-solve-your-hardest-problems/ · https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/pricing · https://github.com/google/adk-python/commit/1754b3eeb6cdb2c16e3b30619a12066623df132e · https://deepmind.google/models/model-cards/gemini-4-argon/ 7. RSI4EO uses coding agents and sealed verifiers to build Earth-observation models Desk: agents_memory Evidence: A · credible_unconfirmed · active · importance 6/10 (Major) Importance rationale: If the paper’s results hold under independent, matched evaluation, automated coding agents could lower the labeled-data and engineering burden for Earth-observation model development across several operationally relevant tasks. A 6 reflects meaningful domain and workflow potential, while the single paper, narrow task suite, unverifiable harness details at present and absent replication limit broader consequence claims. What changed: An October 13 arXiv paper introduces RSI4EO, a benchmark and agent workflow in which GPT-6 Astra builds end-to-end Earth-observation model pipelines using a constrained coding harness and sealed task verifiers. The authors report that the agent exceeds published full-label baselines on four benchmarks, and that few-label runs retain 69–84% of full-label accuracy while using 0.2–1.4% of labels. The fifth benchmark lacks a same-protocol published comparator. These are paper-reported results: the linked project repository was empty when inspected, and no independent reproduction was run. Why it matters: If independently reproduced, this would show a coding agent can assemble useful remote-sensing pipelines under constrained data access, with reported accuracy approaching full-label training from very small labeled subsets. The benchmark’s verifier and data-generation setup may enable repeatable research, but reproduction, verifier-query accounting and matched baselines are needed to assess how much of the result transfers beyond the paper’s harness. Claimed: The authors report that GPT-6 Astra-built pipelines outperform published full-label results on four benchmarks. In few-label settings they report 69–84% of full-label accuracy using 0.2–1.4% of the labels. One benchmark has no same-protocol published comparator. Mechanism: RSI4EO formulates each Earth-observation task as a constrained harness with a sealed verifier. The coding agent can inspect the permitted training data, construct and run a pipeline, and query the verifier to assess submitted outputs. The paper evaluates full-label and few-label settings across five benchmark tasks. Strongest baseline: The paper compares with published full-label results and its own full-label condition. Baseline protocols and task settings are not uniformly matched; the fifth benchmark has no published comparator using the reported protocol. Regime: Five Earth-observation benchmark tasks using a constrained coding-agent harness, task-specific datasets and sealed verifiers; one run per agent per task as described by the paper. Limitations: All performance results are reported by the paper authors and were not independently reproduced in this run.; The linked project repository was empty at inspection; the task package, pipeline code and complete run traces were not available there.; One benchmark lacks a same-protocol published comparator, and other published baseline protocols may differ from the paper’s setup.; A complete verifier-query budget and cost accounting were not established from the inspected materials; verifier use and data access are important to interpreting the results. Open evidence gaps: No independent reproduction of the reported benchmark scores or few-label results was completed, and the linked code repository was empty at inspection.; Published comparison protocols are not uniformly matched, and one benchmark has no same-protocol published comparator.; The available materials do not establish a complete verifier query cap, data leakage audit or cost breakdown. Sources: https://arxiv.org/html/2610.18845 · https://github.com/Yokoya-Lab-UTokyo/RSI4EO 8. RLVR rollout batches trade sample efficiency against training stability Desk: reasoning_posttraining Evidence: A · credible_unconfirmed · active · importance 6/10 (Major) Importance rationale: If the paper's measured batch-size and failure laws generalize beyond its tested model family and task, they change how RLVR practitioners choose rollout batch sizes and learning-rate schedules, affecting sample use and stability during costly post-training. The practical consequence is meaningful but bounded by one principal task domain and unmeasured compute and wall-clock efficiency. What changed: An arXiv paper reports controlled GRPO experiments on Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B and related checkpoints. Across 21 unclipped runs spanning a 32-fold optimizer-batch range and nearly sixfold learning-rate range, the authors find that training failure timing is more consistent with consumed response samples than optimizer steps along square-root learning-rate scaling. They also report declining sample efficiency above a learning-rate-dependent critical batch, with clipping delaying failure but not removing the progress gap. The results are author-reported and have not been independently reproduced. Why it matters: Large rollout batches are used to increase RLVR training throughput, but this paper reports that sample efficiency can worsen above a critical batch size while instability tracks consumed samples. If the pattern transfers, batch selection and schedule design may need to account for both clocks; the paper does not measure wall-clock or compute savings. Demonstrated: The paper reports controlled experiments including 21 unclipped runs across a 32-fold batch range, additional clipped runs, and checkpoint comparisons. These are author-reported experiments, not independent verification. Claimed: For tested GRPO settings, the paper reports that sample efficiency declines above a learning-rate-dependent critical rollout batch, while unclipped failure timing approximately follows consumed response samples along square-root learning-rate scaling. Mechanism: A local quadratic progress model predicts curvature-related loss at large batches; a separate drift-threshold account predicts a failure clock tied to consumed samples. Ratio clipping may delay instability, especially at larger batches, while leaving the sample-efficiency gap. Strongest baseline: Matched smaller and larger rollout batches under square-root learning-rate scaling, with clipped and unclipped comparisons and checkpoint robustness tests. Regime: GRPO/RLVR training on Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B with related Qwen2.5 checkpoints and math tasks; batch, learning rate, clipping and response-sample budgets varied. Limitations: Results are author-reported and not independently reproduced.; The main experiments use one model family and a narrow task domain; cross-family transfer is not established.; Efficiency is measured in generated responses, not tokens, compute cost, throughput or wall-clock time.; Failure timing varies across seeds, and some runs are censored by the training budget.; The paper's local theory is evaluated through predictions; the curvature term is not directly measured at this scale. Open evidence gaps: Independent reproduction of the batch/rate sweep and the claimed sample-efficiency and failure-timing behavior.; Generalization beyond the tested Qwen2.5 family and mathematical reasoning task domain is unmeasured. Sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18853 9. Theory paper separates parallelism limits across diffusion language model paradigms Desk: architectures_scaling Evidence: A · credible_unconfirmed · active · importance 6/10 (Major) Importance rationale: If the conditional theoretical results apply to trained diffusion language models, they change the understanding of how diffusion paradigms trade sampling parallelism under score error. The result is significant for architecture and inference theory, but its practical relevance depends on oracle assumptions and has not been measured in deployed models. What changed: A September 2026 theory paper compares parallel sampling complexity for masked, uniform and Gaussian diffusion. It proves that, under stated score-estimation assumptions, uniform and Gaussian samplers can scale forward-pass complexity with the target distribution's dual total correlation. For a specified family of random empirical measures, the authors give Õ(√d) necessary-and-sufficient pass complexity for uniform or Gaussian diffusion, while constructing approximate score oracles for which masked diffusion requires Õ(d) passes. They attribute the separation to narrower critical windows in the masked process.
