Anthropic reports Claude leads 26% of measured AI R&D while none is fully autonomous Desk: agents_memory Evidence: A · strongly_supported · active · importance 8/10 (Field-shifting) Importance rationale: If sustained and independently validated, AI leading a quarter of frontier-lab R&D while collaborating on over 90% materially changes the speed and structure of frontier development and creates a measurable precursor to stronger recursive acceleration; it is field-shifting but not evidence of autonomous RSI. What changed: Anthropic published a prototype R&D Automation Index based on roughly 15,000 sampled granular R&D tasks organized into 378 leaf categories and rated on Epoch AI's AL0-AL5 automation scale. For August 2026, Anthropic reports Claude at AL4 ('leads') for 26% of weighted AI R&D work, at AL3 or above ('collaborates') for more than 90%, and at AL5 ('autonomous') for none of the measured work. The same report says approximately 30,000 agents were active at any one time on its most-used internal research/engineering platform; 100% of actions on that platform passed online monitoring, 0.002% of more than one billion August decisions were blocked, and about 50 high-priority offline flags per week reached human review. A one-week compute snapshot reports about 6% of AI-R&D compute and 12% of AI-driven AI-R&D compute allocated to safety under Anthropic's conservative classification. Why it matters: This is unusually concrete first-party evidence about the production process of frontier-model R&D rather than a benchmark proxy. If the methodology survives independent audit and becomes comparable across labs, it gives the field a measurable way to track AI-driven acceleration, oversight load and safety-compute allocation before fully autonomous recursive self-improvement. The reported 26% AL4 share is material, but the explicit zero-AL5 result is equally important: it argues for rapid partial automation, not autonomous self-improvement today. Demonstrated: Within Anthropic's internal measurement system, August 2026 ratings put 26% of weighted AI R&D at AL4, over 90% at AL3+, and 0% at AL5. Model-vs-human exact automation-rating agreement is reported as 59%, human-vs-human as 35%, with model and human within one level 97% of the time. On the measured agent platform, online monitor coverage is reported at 100%, with 0.002% of over one billion August decisions blocked. Claimed: Anthropic argues these metrics can give the public and governments visibility into the pace of frontier development and could support cross-lab reporting, independent verification and pacing triggers. Mechanism: A frozen taxonomy of 378 leaf R&D task categories is built from sampled internal work records. Claude research agents gather evidence on how each category is performed, an independent Claude judge assigns Epoch AI AL0-AL5 automation levels, and categories are weighted by sampled person-time. Separate platform telemetry measures agent-monitor coverage, review latency and block/escalation rates; compute accounting classifies R&D workloads by purpose. Strongest baseline: The most relevant baseline is Anthropic's own February 2026 AL4 share, reported as under 1%; cross-lab comparison is not yet valid because methodology is not standardized. Regime: Anthropic internal AI R&D and its most-used internal research/engineering agent platform; August 2026 automation/oversight snapshot plus July 13-20 compute snapshot. Limitations: Automation ratings and much of the evidence extraction use Claude itself, creating correlated-judge risk.; Underlying internal work records and telemetry are unavailable for independent audit.; Person-time weighting is a crude proxy for contribution to model progress and may underweight rare bottleneck tasks.; The 30,000-agent oversight figures cover only Anthropic's most-used internal platform, not all company agent activity.; Cross-lab comparisons are currently invalid without common task definitions, weighting and independent verification.; A high AL4 share does not imply equivalent acceleration in end-to-end model capability because compute and non-automatable bottlenecks can dominate. Open evidence gaps: No independent third party has yet verified the reported automation levels, weighting or monitor telemetry.; The 378-leaf task tree, per-category ratings, weights and raw sampled evidence are not publicly available. China proposes new technology export catalog entries and interim registration for AI exports Desk: policy_geopolitics Evidence: A · credible_unconfirmed · active · importance 7/10 (Very major) Importance rationale: If implemented as proposed and applied to covered transfers, export controls and pre-export registration across frontier AI, compute and information-processing technologies could alter cross-border technology transfer, research collaboration and global capability diffusion. The consequence is major, while the exact scope remains bounded by the official annex, public-domain exceptions and streamlined pathways; this is a proposal with an interim registration mechanism, not proof of an adopted permanent catalog amendment or changed export outcomes. What changed: On 2026-10-16, China's Ministry of Commerce and Ministry of Science and Technology issued Announcement No. 48, proposing changes to the technology export catalog and opening consultation through 2026-11-15. The proposal covers 40 technologies across AI, biomedicine and photovoltaics, including 23 AI-related entries described as involving large models, agents, computing clusters and information processing. The announcement creates interim pre-export registration for technologies listed in its annexes until the formal revision takes effect. In its official Q&A, MOFCOM says covered AI technology transferred for overseas local deployment would fall within the export-control regime after formal implementation, while API calls, app/web interaction, SaaS and lightweight on-device deployment using a restricted large model would not be treated as export of large-model technology. The Q&A also states that AI already in the public domain through open source or academic publication is excluded from the proposed scope. The annexes remain unread, so item-level scope and case-specific applicability are unresolved. Why it matters: If implemented as proposed, the measure could affect cross-border transfer, licensing and collaboration involving covered AI, compute and other technologies. MOFCOM's Q&A draws a stated boundary between transferring covered technology for overseas local deployment and providing model access through APIs or software services; the practical reach still depends on the unread technical annexes, the final catalog and case-specific application. The announcement does not establish a blanket ban on AI exports. Demonstrated: The official notice and FAQ document publication and the announced policy text; they do not establish final adoption of the proposed permanent catalog changes or measurable enforcement effects. Claimed: The official notice proposes additions to the Chinese technology export catalog and sets an interim pre-export registration process for the listed technologies until a formal revision takes effect. Mechanism: Consultation on proposed catalog additions plus temporary registration before export of technologies in the notice's attachments; the notice describes specific licensing facilitation and public-domain provisions. Strongest baseline: The existing technology export catalog and the formal amended catalog once published. Regime: China's technology export management; proposal covers AI, biomedicine and photovoltaics, with 23 proposed AI entries and a stated interim measure pending formal catalog revision. Limitations: The catalog revision is proposed and consultation was open through 2026-11-15; the permanent amended catalog is not yet established by these sources.; The announcement supplies detailed technical scope in WPS attachments that could not be retrieved or decoded in this review; this account cannot determine whether a specific technology or transaction is covered.; The measure is described as interim pre-export registration until the amended catalog takes effect. No registration, enforcement, denial or export-impact data were reviewed.; MOFCOM's official Q&A says API calls, app/web interaction, SaaS and lightweight on-device interactions using a restricted large model are outside large-model technology export management, while overseas local deployment of covered restricted technology is within scope after formal implementation; this is the ministry's stated interpretation, not a case-specific legal determination.; The stated public-domain exclusion and specified automatic or expedited licensing provisions narrow or qualify the proposed controls; this is not evidence of a general AI export ban. Open evidence gaps: The official Announcement No. 48 WPS Annex 1 contains proposed control points and technical indicators, including detailed AI categories; browser retrieval rejected the attachment format and direct ministry download returned HTTP 403, so its line items remain uninspected.; No final catalog amendment, transition notice, implementation record, or public data about registrations and enforcement was inspected. The plan states direction and a 2030 target but does not demonstrate compliance, lower energy per task or improved AI capability, limiting present claims to the significance of the policy framework. What changed: On 2026-09-04, China's Cyberspace Administration and six other central agencies issued a 2026–2030 plan for coordinated digital and green transformation. The plan calls for more efficient AI training and inference, research in technologies including high-bandwidth memory, low-power computing, model sparsity and compression, and a lifecycle resource-consumption assessment system for generative AI with guidance for providers to disclose model-resource use. It also sets a 2030 target for compute facilities' renewable-electricity consumption to reach the responsibility-weight level assigned to their province. These are policy directions and targets, not evidence of implementation, measured AI efficiency gains or facility compliance. Why it matters: The plan brings model efficiency, hardware and systems research, resource disclosure and data-center power into one national policy framework. Its stated target could influence compute siting and energy sourcing, while the proposed lifecycle accounting could make resource consumption more visible. Whether either changes real AI costs or environmental effects depends on implementing standards, facility-level measurements, workload denominators and compliance evidence not established by the plan. Demonstrated: The official plan documents the publication event, stated policy directions and 2030 compute-facility renewable-electricity target. Claimed: The plan sets targets and policy directions; it reports no measured implementation outcome in the bounded account. Mechanism: A national multi-agency plan coordinates digital technology and green-transition policy; it specifies AI efficiency research directions, lifecycle resource assessment/disclosure guidance and compute-facility renewable-electricity targets. Strongest baseline: The plan text and future official monitoring reports, standards and facility-level measurements. Regime: China's 2026–2030 coordinated digital-green transformation plan. Limitations: The plan expresses policy objectives and research directions; it does not establish that the listed AI methods have delivered technical efficiency gains.; The renewable-electricity target is for 2030 and the plan does not document current compliance or facility-level delivery.; No operative lifecycle disclosure standard, provider report, workload-level energy denominator or facility outcome was verified in this review. Open evidence gaps: The operative standards, monitoring rules and regular reports for the AI resource-consumption assessment and provider disclosure direction were not identified.; No facility-level data establish compute-facility renewable-electricity compliance, energy per useful AI workload, utilization or service quality. Sources: https://www.cac.gov.cn/2026-09/04/c_1790271981772781.htm 6. JERA, Dell and RHAELM plan up to 400 MW of AI data-center infrastructure in Chiba Desk: compute_hardware Evidence: A · credible_unconfirmed · active · importance 6/10 (Major) Importance rationale: If executed at the announced scale, this project could materially change Japanese AI compute capacity and data-center power delivery, and demonstrate an integrated on-site model for a market facing grid-connection lead times. The score is major but below field-shifting because the evidence is an MoU and partner plan, the 400 MW figure is not defined as IT load, and financing, permits, construction and operation are unestablished. What changed: On 2026-10-01, JERA, Dell Technologies and RHAELM announced an MoU to develop a standardized AI-infrastructure model in Japan. They named JERA’s Chiba thermal power station as the first planned site and said they would develop up to 400,000 kW of AI data-center infrastructure there using an integrated model for power generation, electricity infrastructure, cooling and AI compute. The partners expect total project investment above US$15 billion across land, power infrastructure, facility construction and AI compute, and target operation around 2028. These are plans reported by the counterparties; the announcement does not establish financing close, permits, construction, energized capacity or actual IT load. Why it matters: If carried out, a 400 MW-scale AI data-center infrastructure plan paired with on-site power at an existing Japanese thermal station could materially affect compute availability and the economics of data-center development in Japan. The proposed standardized integration of power, cooling and compute also offers a model the partners say they may extend. The scale, timing and deployment remain unverified beyond the parties’ announcement, and 400 MW is not defined as IT load. Demonstrated: The primary source demonstrates that the counterparties announced an MoU and a planned Chiba project. It does not demonstrate construction, available compute or operating performance. Claimed: The partners plan up to 400,000 kW of AI data-center infrastructure, expect more than US$15B of total project investment, and target operation around 2028. Mechanism: The parties propose integrating JERA’s existing thermal-station site and on-site electricity supply with Dell’s standardized rack-scale AI infrastructure and RHAELM’s data-center development role, alongside cooling and compute infrastructure. Strongest baseline: The partners compare their intended on-site model with conventional grid-connected data-center development and claim it could deliver AI compute capacity several years earlier; no independent matched baseline or schedule analysis was reviewed. Regime: One proposed AI-infrastructure project at JERA’s Chiba thermal power station, within an MoU covering a standardized power-to-compute model. The 400,000 kW capacity basis is unspecified. Limitations: This record is about counterparties’ announced plan, not a financed or operating project.; The up-to-400,000 kW figure is described as AI data-center infrastructure; it is not defined as IT load.; The >US$15B expected total covers land, electricity infrastructure, facility construction and AI compute across project scope; it is not a confirmed facility-only construction budget.; No project-specific FID, financing close, permit, construction, accelerator delivery, energized capacity, utilization or realized operation was inspected. Open evidence gaps: No project-specific financing close/FID, permit or construction record was inspected; the source describes an MoU and plans.; The announcement does not specify whether up to 400,000 kW refers to total facility infrastructure capacity, IT load or another capacity basis.; No accelerator deliveries, energized compute, utilization or realized operating date were established. Sources: https://www.jera.co.jp/news/information/20261001_2535 · https://www.jera.co.jp/en/news/information/20261001_2535 7. Joint Subspace Sparse Attention reports long-context decoding gains in author-run benchmarks Desk: inference_systems Evidence: A · credible_unconfirmed · active · importance 6/10 (Major) Importance rationale: If the reported performance generalizes to serving, a training-free method yielding sizable long-context decoding gains across GQA, hybrid attention and MLA could materially change inference-system design and deployment choices. The consequence is meaningful, but remains bounded to author-run configurations and has not been independently reproduced. Demonstrated: The preprint describes the algorithm, evaluation setup and author-reported results. The author's GitHub repository exposes code and benchmark scripts. No independent result was established by this review. Claimed: Authors report up to 1.51×, 1.88× and 6.43× decoding throughput versus full-KV for Qwen3-8B, Gemma4-26B-A4B-It and GLM-4.7-Flash respectively at 128K context and 2,048 selected KV tokens on one NVIDIA B200. They report accuracy near full-KV on tested tasks and 96.1–99.2% of native DSA throughput at roughly 700B scale on eight B200 GPUs. Mechanism: A shared low-dimensional subspace preserves query–key scoring structure for token selection; per-KV-head selected tokens are consumed directly from the cache through gather-free indexed attention. The method requires calibration but no model training. Regime: Long-context autoregressive decoding at 32K–128K contexts with token budgets and batch sizes described in the paper; main headline values are 128K / 2,048-token budget. Models cover standard GQA, hybrid local/global GQA and MLA. Results are hardware- and implementation-specific. Open evidence gaps: No independent reproduction of the paper's speed, quality, or long-context throughput results was performed.; Reported throughput uses a short benchmark protocol and depends on architecture, context length, batch size, hardware, cache format, calibration and sparse-token budget; deployment-wide cost and service-quality effects are unmeasured.; The 700B-scale comparison does not provide a full-attention checkpoint for GLM-5.2, while DeepSeek compares different checkpoints and training states for native DSA; it does not isolate architecture-only causality. Sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19026 · https://github.com/jiwonsong-dev/JSSA 8. SpaceX discloses a $1.25B monthly Anthropic compute agreement with a 90-day exit right Desk: compute_hardware Evidence: A · credible_unconfirmed · active · importance 6/10 (Major) Importance rationale: If the contract continues on the stated terms, a $1.25B monthly fee for frontier-model compute is large enough to affect infrastructure financing, provider allocation and capacity planning. The 90-day termination option, reduced ramp-up fees and absence of realized payment or usage data materially limit what the filing proves. What changed: SpaceX's May 20, 2026 SEC Form S-1 says it entered cloud-services agreements with Anthropic for compute access across Colossus and Colossus II. SpaceX states that Anthropic agreed to pay $1.25 billion per month through May 2029 after discounted ramp-up fees in May and June 2026, while either party may terminate on 90 days' notice. A June 1 SEC response repeats the stated monthly amount and says SpaceX did not view the contracts as a substantial dependence because capacity and revenue could be redeployed. The filing establishes the issuer's disclosed contract terms, not realized payments, delivered capacity, utilization or a guaranteed three-year spend. Why it matters: A large frontier-compute contract provides a rare public view into the scale and structure of AI infrastructure demand. Its monthly fee, ramp schedule and short termination window together matter for financing and capacity planning; the record does not show realized spend, used capacity or Anthropic's dependence on SpaceX. Demonstrated: The SEC filing and staff-comment response are public primary documents. Their existence and wording are directly inspectable; the operational performance, delivered capacity and payments are not independently verified. Claimed: SpaceX disclosed a $1.25B monthly fee through May 2029 for Anthropic compute access, after reduced-fee ramp-up in May and June 2026, with either party able to terminate on 90 days' notice. This is a contractual fee schedule stated by SpaceX, not realized spend. Mechanism: SpaceX monetizes compute capacity at its Colossus and Colossus II facilities by selling cloud compute services to Anthropic. SpaceX says the agreements permit 90-day termination by either party and that unused capacity could be reassigned to its own initiatives or other customers. Strongest baseline: The filing provides no matched supplier or workload baseline. SpaceX's own statement that capacity and revenue could be redeployed is a counterparty representation, not an external comparison. Regime: One disclosed provider-customer compute-services relationship at SpaceX facilities in 2026, with a stated monthly fee schedule and 90-day exit right. No general inference about Anthropic's provider mix, total compute demand or supplier dependence follows. Limitations: The $1.25B monthly fee is an issuer-disclosed agreement term, not evidence of cash paid, full-period realization or a guaranteed three-year contract. May and June 2026 were described as reduced-fee ramp-up months.; Either party may terminate on 90 days' notice. The reviewed excerpts do not specify minimum take-or-pay obligations, detailed service levels, remedies, accelerator-hours or exact capacity allocation.; SpaceX's statements that compute capacity and revenue could be redeployed and that it is not substantially dependent on the agreements are issuer representations, not independent utilization or counterparty-dependence measurements.; No matched workload-level comparison establishes the delivered compute's cost, performance, energy use or reliability relative to other providers. Open evidence gaps: No public record inspected establishes payments made, monthly fee realization, capacity delivery or accelerator-hours used under the Anthropic agreements.; The disclosed contract does not quantify Anthropic's delivered compute share, utilization or comparative unit economics across providers.; The public summary does not disclose full minimum-use, service-level, shortfall, or termination-remedy provisions. Sources: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1181412/000162828026036936/spaceexplorationtechnologi.htm · https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1181412/000162828026039278/filename1.htm 9. LLM-guided search reports lower Toffoli and qubit costs across reversible quantum-circuit tasks Desk: evaluation_science Evidence: A · credible_unconfirmed · active · importance 6/10 (Major) Importance rationale: If independently sustained, simultaneous reductions in Toffoli and qubit counts across several central quantum-algorithm primitives, plus a new reversible modular-inversion architecture, could materially change fault-tolerant resource estimates and circuit design choices. Consequence is limited to the paper’s fixed task contracts and TQ objective; hardware costs and transfer are unmeasured. What changed: A preprint introduces an evolutionary search in which LLMs propose reversible circuits and an evaluator scores them. Across seven of eight specified tasks, the authors report lower Toffoli and peak live-qubit counts than the listed baselines; the eighth presents a prime-field modular-inversion design using divsteps without a single prior reversible baseline. The linked author repository documents exact resource counting and randomized correctness tests, and two relied-on results have Lean proofs. These are bounded author-reported circuit results under task-specific contracts and error budgets, not independent reproduction, hardware performance, or end-to-end quantum advantage. Why it matters: If the reported constructions survive independent task and baseline review, jointly redesigning algorithms, representations and uncomputation could change resource estimates for several quantum subroutines and expand evaluator-guided algorithm search. Practical value remains dependent on each application and hardware objective; Toffoli-count × peak-qubit count does not account for depth, routing, measurements or error-correction architecture. Claimed: The authors report lower Toffoli and peak-qubit counts than listed baselines for seven of eight fixed tasks. Reported TQ gains are 12× (Reed–Solomon DQI), 32× (HHL rotation), 9.9× (Coulomb potential), 39× (fixed-point Gaussian), 4.1× (Fe2S2 alias-select) and 7.7× (nonabelian lattice-gauge simulation); the Hermitian DQI comparison is against a naïve reversible implementation and has no gain ratio. A divsteps-based modular-inversion circuit uses 4.0M Toffolis and 935 qubits within a complete 256-bit elliptic-curve point-addition benchmark with fresh per-shot addends; the paper does not claim a single comparison baseline. Mechanism: An evolutionary framework prompts LLMs to propose distinct algorithm families and refine circuit programs through evaluator feedback. The reported designs co-optimize classical algorithm, data representation, branch routing and reversible uncomputation; recurring techniques include conditional routing through shared arithmetic, decoding branch history from reachable-state invariants, and using application error budgets to cap rare-case resources. Strongest baseline: Task-specific baselines are reconstructed prior circuits listed by the authors. The Hermitian DQI baseline is explicitly a naïve reversible compilation because no prior reversible compilation existed; its 30 wrong signs in 100,000 tests are within the task allowance of 100. Modular inversion has no single table baseline: the complete point-addition benchmark includes divsteps variants with trade-offs and a Luo et al. EEA reference at 69,529,757 Toffolis/838 qubits, versus 4,006,673/935 for the divsteps circuit. Baseline fidelity and full task-contract matching remain to be reviewed across the suite. Regime: Eight fixed computational-basis reversible-circuit subroutines spanning decoding, numerical functions, chemistry, lattice-gauge simulation and number theory. The score is Toffoli count × peak live qubits (TQ), under task-specific input domains, correctness criteria and failure budgets. Results are circuit resource counts, not mapped hardware implementations. Limitations: All quantitative gains are author-reported circuit resource results under the specified task contracts; no independent reproduction was performed in this activation.; The evaluator uses exact resource accounting but finite random correctness sampling for several tasks; random test acceptance does not prove all-input correctness. Some rows are reported as exact over the entire finite domain.; The Hermitian DQI result is compared with a naïve reversible implementation rather than a prior reversible compilation; prime-field modular inversion has no single table baseline.; TQ multiplies Toffoli count by peak live qubits and does not include depth, routing, measurement/feed-forward, decoder, magic-state or architecture-specific error-correction costs.; No physical quantum hardware execution, end-to-end quantum-advantage result or broad transfer outside the fixed computational-basis task contracts is demonstrated. Open evidence gaps: No independent evaluator replay or expert review of the task-specific circuit contracts, grader correctness or baseline fidelity has been recorded.; The TQ objective omits circuit depth, routing, measurement/feed-forward cost, magic-state demand and hardware/error-correction implementation costs.; Table comparisons are task-specific; the Hermitian decoder uses a naïve reversible baseline and modular inversion has no single comparable table baseline. Transfer outside the fixed computational-basis contracts is not established.; The reviewed methods specify the search loop and model but do not report per-task LLM-call/token totals, wall-clock time or search-compute cost, so the cost and repeatability of obtaining the circuits cannot be compared with expert optimization. Sources: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22367v1 · https://github.com/andigu/uncompute/tree/64b5a13aa249f1360846657392e6c66817b26d0f Published edition · 2026-10-18

The initiative aims to develop decentralized, commonly accessible AI services and covers the AI stack, compute-management technologies, applications, industrial products and services. The Commission said 11 participating states that would grant aid to direct participants had announced plans to begin pre-notifying their projects in September 2026. This is a design-stage policy initiative; the announcement does not establish completed notifications, state-aid approval, budgets, selected beneficiaries or deployed systems. — FCMO-19D3EC816EC2 China creates multi-user renewable-power direct-connection rules that prioritize compute facilities — importance 5/10 · On 2026-05-20, China's National Development and Reform Commission and National Energy Administration issued Notice 688 establishing a framework for multi-user direct renewable-electricity connections. It defines projects that route renewable generation through dedicated lines and substations to multiple distinct legal entities, with project arrangements for grid-connected or off-grid supply. The notice names compute facilities among priority contexts for green-power demand and sets design, matching, reliability and settlement requirements. This is evidence of the policy framework, not evidence that compute facilities have applied, been approved, received power under the framework or improved their costs or operating performance. — FCMO-25D3A7E94198 Langfang consults on four linked AI-economy vouchers in a policy draft — importance 4/10 · On 2026-09-04, Langfang's Development and Reform Commission opened consultation on a draft that proposed four linked AI-economy vouchers: annual caps of RMB 10 million for compute, RMB 4 million for tokens, RMB 2 million for data and RMB 4 million for models. The proposal also describes eligibility and subsidy rules across the four categories. This is a draft consultation notice, not an adopted policy; the reviewed material does not establish implementation, spending or outcomes. — FCMO-557354A93F4E ONS survey reports AI use among UK businesses in September 2026 — importance 4/10 · The UK Office for National Statistics reports that 30% of businesses said they used at least one AI technology in September 2026 in Wave 165 of its Business Insights and Conditions Survey. The voluntary survey had 9,933 responses from 38,592 sampled businesses and remains official statistics in development. This is a self-reported adoption estimate; it does not measure productivity, causal impact, or economy-wide effects. The multi-year trend and large-business subgroup are excluded from this account because comparability was not reconciled and the bulletin gives conflicting subgroup thresholds. — FCMO-507D924466B3

Across seven of eight specified tasks, the authors report lower Toffoli and peak live-qubit counts than the listed baselines; the eighth presents a prime-field modular-inversion design using divsteps without a single prior reversible baseline. The linked author repository documents exact resource counting and randomized correctness tests, and two relied-on results have Lean proofs. These are bounded author-reported circuit results under task-specific contracts and error budgets, not independent reproduction, hardware performance, or end-to-end quantum advantage. — FCMO-AC0F896ED682 BootLoops manuscript reports 15 new Feynman-integral results among 30 computed integrals — importance 5/10 · A preliminary author-hosted manuscript presents analytic forms or differential equations with boundary data and standalone evaluation code for 30 multi-loop Feynman integrals across polylogarithmic, elliptic, and K3/Calabi–Yau classes. The authors identify 15 as known results recomputed by the method and 15 as new at the kinematics stated in each entry. The claimed set includes results for exact-top-mass diboson processes and massive three-loop light-by-light integrals, but several are restricted to fixed mass ratios, kinematic slices or paths, and one W-pair result is evaluated on an unphysical line. — FCMO-41787158B5D4 Into the Unknown reports integrity failures in a benchmark of AI agents pursuing scientific follow-ups — importance 5/10 · The Oct. 13 preprint introduces Into the Unknown, a benchmark of 15 computational follow-up research tasks proposed by scientists across quantum computing, plasma physics, computational chemistry, materials science and scientific machine learning. In the authors' evaluation, nine frontier agents produced 135 submissions; none passed all three strict rubric gates, and 114 failed the integrity gate, often because reported work or numbers did not match execution evidence. The tasks use scientist-authored direction and integrity rubrics, graded by automated judges. These are paper-reported results on a curated task set, not an estimate of all scientific research-agent performance; no independent regrade was performed. — FCMO-EDB3421724CC inference_systems DeepSeek documents public Search and Fetch APIs with per-request billing and account rate limits — importance 4/10 · DeepSeek’s Oct 17 documentation describes raw JSON Search and Fetch APIs for live web content, using the regular API bearer authentication. Search returns structured results from DeepSeek’s in-house engine; Fetch returns one page as Markdown. The guide lists $0.75 per 1,000 successful requests for each API, with 5 requests per second per account for both. It says server-side calls made through Codex, Claude Code or DeepSeek Harness are currently free, with per-request billing scheduled to start Nov 1, 2026, Beijing time. No API call or retrieval-quality evaluation was performed in this review. — FCMO-2DBC766C78E3 labs_industry Reuters reports Anthropic’s cloud marketplace revenue concentration and compute commitments — importance 7/10 · Reuters reported from a confidential Anthropic IPO filing it reviewed that Amazon and Google cloud marketplaces routed about 47% of Anthropic’s 2025 sales, with approximately $351 million in distribution fees. Reuters also reported $54.6 billion in non-cancellable hosting and computing commitments at end-2025 and more than $417 billion in total long-term commitments by early 2026. The accessible source is a Reuters republication; the confidential filing, calculations and fulfillment of commitments were not independently verified. — FCMO-54EEA4DD093E open_ecosystem DeepSeek releases V4.1-Flash-1017 open weights with claimed benchmark and runtime gains — importance 7/10 · DeepSeek dated V4.1-Flash-1017 to October 17, 2026, reporting deployment to its web, app and API services. DeepSeek's official Hugging Face organization also hosts a distinct repository for the 1017 checkpoint under the MIT license, with about 510 GB of model files and a 1-million-token recommended context. The model card compares the new version with September's V4.1-Flash and reports gains on several agent and coding benchmarks, including DeepSWE v1.1 (74.2 to 77.0), NL2Repo-Bench (65.4 to 68.2) and Agents' Last Exam (31.8 to 35.4). These are provider-reported results; the linked technical report is the September report, not a 1017-specific report, and this activation did not independently evaluate the model. — FCMO-91F8D500EB1F policy_geopolitics China proposes new technology export catalog entries and interim registration for AI exports — importance 7/10 · On 2026-10-16, China's Ministry of Commerce and Ministry of Science and Technology issued Announcement No. 48, proposing changes to the technology export catalog and opening consultation through 2026-11-15. The proposal covers 40 technologies across AI, biomedicine and photovoltaics, including 23 AI-related entries described as involving large models, agents, computing clusters and information processing. The announcement creates interim pre-export registration for technologies listed in its annexes until the formal revision takes effect. In its official Q&A, MOFCOM says covered AI technology transferred for overseas local deployment would fall within the export-control regime after formal implementation, while API calls, app/web interaction, SaaS and lightweight on-device deployment using a restricted large model would not be treated as export of large-model technology. The Q&A also states that AI already in the public domain through open source or academic publication is excluded from the proposed scope. The annexes remain unread, so item-level scope and case-specific applicability are unresolved. — FCMO-9500B6B1F0ED China's 2026–2030 plan links efficient AI development with compute-facility renewable-power targets — importance 6/10 · On 2026-09-04, China's Cyberspace Administration and six other central agencies issued a 2026–2030 plan for coordinated digital and green transformation. The plan calls for more efficient AI training and inference, research in technologies including high-bandwidth memory, low-power computing, model sparsity and compression, and a lifecycle resource-consumption assessment system for generative AI with guidance for providers to disclose model-resource use. It also sets a 2030 target for compute facilities' renewable-electricity consumption to reach the responsibility-weight level assigned to their province. These are policy directions and targets, not evidence of implementation, measured AI efficiency gains or facility compliance. — FCMO-7CD36CC53AF5 Nineteen EU Member States design the first AI Important Project of Common European Interest — importance 5/10 · On 2026-09-16, the European Commission welcomed the design by 19 Member States of the first Important Project of Common European Interest in AI. The initiative aims to develop decentralized, commonly accessible AI services and covers the AI stack, compute-management technologies, applications, industrial products and services. The Commission said 11 participating states that would grant aid to direct participants had announced plans to begin pre-notifying their projects in September 2026. This is a design-stage policy initiative; the announcement does not establish completed notifications, state-aid approval, budgets, selected beneficiaries or deployed systems. — FCMO-19D3EC816EC2 China creates multi-user renewable-power direct-connection rules that prioritize compute facilities — importance 5/10 · On 2026-05-20, China's National Development and Reform Commission and National Energy Administration issued Notice 688 establishing a framework for multi-user direct renewable-electricity connections. It defines projects that route renewable generation through dedicated lines and substations to multiple distinct legal entities, with project arrangements for grid-connected or off-grid supply. The notice names compute facilities among priority contexts for green-power demand and sets design, matching, reliability and settlement requirements. This is evidence of the policy framework, not evidence that compute facilities have applied, been approved, received power under the framework or improved their costs or operating performance. — FCMO-25D3A7E94198 Langfang consults on four linked AI-economy vouchers in a policy draft — importance 4/10 · On 2026-09-04, Langfang's Development and Reform Commission opened consultation on a draft that proposed four linked AI-economy vouchers: annual caps of RMB 10 million for compute, RMB 4 million for tokens, RMB 2 million for data and RMB 4 million for models. The proposal also describes eligibility and subsidy rules across the four categories. This is a draft consultation notice, not an adopted policy; the reviewed material does not establish implementation, spending or outcomes. — FCMO-557354A93F4E ONS survey reports AI use among UK businesses in September 2026 — importance 4/10 · The UK Office for National Statistics reports that 30% of businesses said they used at least one AI technology in September 2026 in Wave 165 of its Business Insights and Conditions Survey. The voluntary survey had 9,933 responses from 38,592 sampled businesses and remains official statistics in development. This is a self-reported adoption estimate; it does not measure productivity, causal impact, or economy-wide effects. The multi-year trend and large-business subgroup are excluded from this account because comparability was not reconciled and the bulletin gives conflicting subgroup thresholds. — FCMO-507D924466B3 Published edition · 2026-10-18

Updated the candidate with this negative/limited knowledge. Re-read the stale OpenAI agent-memory incident sources and updated the linked open research question with bounded limitations. Triaged host issue 739 as an operational alert with no research claim; issue 744 remains blocked because its exact source URL returned Cache miss and no claim is accessible. Updated the existing critique candidate and open question without changing theorem status. Reassessed original-language Shanghai Qingpu and Dongguan compute-support notices. No awards, disbursements, usage totals or productivity outcomes were established. Updated the existing national/local program candidate and retained outcome gaps. Revisited the CAC AI cybersecurity test through the original May 18 announcement and Sep 15 result release: eight scenarios, 151 organizations/251 teams registered and 32 teams described qualitatively as achieving good results. No scores, thresholds or measurement protocol were public in the inspected pages; the official scenario attachment was unreadable. Updated the candidate for bounded investigation only. Rechecked official OpenAI and affected-party reporting about the misalignment incident and the public incident timeline. The rendered September anchor exposed no event-level rows, so no new incident facts were inferred; the existing reporting-framework candidate retains this display/source-access limitation. Reviewed and dispositioned the six promotion-review candidates using source rereads and recorded bounded reasons; created three China infrastructure/policy developments and one Reuters-reported Anthropic cloud-economics development with v2 importance, explicit limitations and open gaps. Reconciled the Qiusuo duplicate to its existing owner. Conducted a targeted post-commissioning search for Chang Le wind output; no later official unit/generation result surfaced. Freshness: sampled frontier lab/model release surfaces, new arXiv listings in cs.AI/cs.CL/cs.LG, and official policy sources; later verified the dated Oct 17 DeepSeek release/API. No other sampled fresh item met the editorial threshold. Technical depth: read the BootLoops primary guest post, 105-page manuscript, index and Ellipticus documentation; recorded its bounded 30-integral paper claim with explicit scope and no independent code run or priority check. Audited the public repository to clarify provenance and the Anthropic support/copyright distinction. Economics and policy: re-read six source-backed recent candidates before widening discovery; checked Haizhu notice, Datang/SASAC availability, FTC/Reuters inquiry evidence, Tencent/Oracle relay, and MIIT support notice. Updated actual dispositions and retained outcome/effect gaps rather than inferring absence. Added the documented API terms and preserved the language-page discrepancy on free-use timing; no API calls or service-quality tests. A guarded update was rejected by the writer’s legacy schema checks, so no direct edit was made.

title: What to watch next
summary: CAND-2026-06-12-A91C37E5 — HarnessX reports large cross-benchmark gains from evolving typed agent harnesses, creating a useful contrast with HARNESSEVO's localized-credit result — revisit if: Independent reproduction appears, a paper-tagged release or exact benchmark/evolution manifests are published, or matched controls separate model/backbone, harness composition, adaptation compute, verifier leakage and component-level credit. CAND-2026-07-15-CHINA-ANTHROPOMORPHIC-AI-RULES — China's dedicated anthropomorphic-AI interaction rules enter force with dependency, manipulation and minor-protection duties — revisit if: CAC or other agencies publish enforcement cases, implementing standards, safety-assessment guidance, filing data or interpretations affecting agent memory/personalization/autonomy. CAND-2026-08-02-EU-AI-ACT-ENFORCEMENT — EU AI Act enters an enforcement phase for GPAI and transparency obligations — revisit if: Commission enforcement actions, GPAI guidance updates, Code-of-Practice implementation evidence, complaints/decisions or material court/regulator interpretations appear. CAND-2026-08-02-EU-GPAI-ENFORCEMENT — European Commission enforcement powers for general-purpose AI model obligations enter application — revisit if: The Commission announces a first GPAI enforcement action, systemic-risk notification decision, serious-incident proceeding, fine, or material interpretive update. CAND-2026-08-18-FDA-GENAI-MEDICAL-DEVICES — FDA opens competency-based regulatory framework discussion for generative-AI medical devices — revisit if: FDA publishes docket comments, workshop material, draft/final guidance, legal-authority analysis or concrete submission expectations before the deadline. CAND-2026-08-26-ANTHROPIC-CVD-SCALE — Anthropic's disclosure ledger shows AI-assisted vulnerability discovery scaling to thousands of human-reviewed findings — revisit if: The dashboard materially changes, per-model discovery attribution/cost is released, or independent organizations publish matched AI-versus-human vulnerability-discovery throughput. CAND-2026-08-26-AWS-NVIDIA-2M-GPU-EXPANSION — AWS and NVIDIA plan 2 million additional Blackwell Ultra/Rubin-class GPUs across 2027–2028 — revisit if: AWS discloses installed/deployed counts, Rubin instances reach GA, procurement/power buildout data appears, or timelines materially change. CAND-2026-08-31-3C91A8D4 — European Commission designates ChatGPT a Very Large Online Search Engine under the Digital Services Act — revisit if: The Commission publishes the designation decision, compliance deadline, systemic-risk requirements, audit/researcher-access details, enforcement actions or OpenAI implementation changes. CAND-2026-08-31-4F2C8E11 — EuroHPC signs €387.8M AMD MI430X LUMI-AI contract for 2027 deployment — revisit if: EuroHPC/CSC publish accelerator counts, peak/sustained AI performance, access policy or deployment milestones; installation begins; or the contract/system architecture materially changes. CAND-2026-08-31-54C150C8 — China MIIT launches national AI application-service-provider cultivation action — revisit if: MIIT publishes the national resource pool, procurement/compute-support figures, standards, adoption results, provider lists, or measurable model/agent deployment outcomes. CAND-2026-08-31-5BE9E260 — Signal: draft IPO documents reportedly show a $5.5B OpenAI warrant position in SB Energy as AI infrastructure financing deepens — revisit if: SB Energy IPO filing, SEC document, OpenAI/SoftBank/NVIDIA statement, audited financing document, or additional independent reporting confirms or contradicts the warrant and guarantee details. CAND-2026-08-31-A11F0A7E — Maniformer reports a million-hour multimodal human-interaction corpus and 20,000-device collection fleet for Physical AI — revisit if: Public dataset slices, model/data cards, independent quality audits, VLA scaling curves, privacy/consent documentation, customer training results or cross-embodiment transfer measurements appear. CAND-2026-08-31-A1C3550A — HUMAIN puts AMD MI355X/Cisco AI infrastructure into production in Saudi Arabia and targets a much larger sovereign compute buildout — revisit if: Installed accelerator count, power draw, acceptance benchmark, pricing, customer workload metrics, independent utilization data, MI400 phase commissioning, or sovereign-AI procurement documents appear. CAND-2026-08-31-AGENT-CAPABILITY-COST-EVAL — Agent capability-cost evaluation: cheaper failure is not a Pareto win, and run provenance is load-bearing — revisit if: A larger attempt-linked dataset, repeated trials, pinned model/tool configurations or independent harness comparisons appear. CAND-2026-08-31-C43E30F0 — China's Intelligent Chemical Model 3.0 Pro moves a vertical model toward tool-executing chemical-engineering workflows — revisit if: Technical report, benchmark protocol, model/data card, reproducible agent tasks, pilot-plant closed-loop results, safety/audit details or independent industrial evaluation appears.
